44  Causal Inference and Field Experiments

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

Marketing decisions are causal claims in disguise. “Spend another dollar on search advertising and we will earn three” is a statement about a counterfactual world that did not happen—the sales the firm would have realized had it not spent the dollar. A correlation between advertising and sales, however precisely estimated, does not license that statement, because the firm chose how much to advertise, and it chose to advertise more precisely where and when it expected to sell more. The gap between what we measure (an association in observational data) and what we want to know (the effect of an intervention we control) is the central problem of this chapter, and of empirical marketing more broadly.

This chapter develops the modern toolkit for closing that gap. It begins with the potential-outcomes framework, the language in which a causal effect is defined before any estimator is chosen, and shows why the naive comparison of treated and untreated units is biased by selection. It then treats randomized experiments and online A/B tests as the benchmark that solves selection by design, and the four leading quasi-experimental designs—difference-in-differences (DiD), instrumental variables (IV), regression discontinuity (RD), and the synthetic control method (SCM)—as strategies for recovering causal effects when randomization is infeasible. Each method is presented the same way: the intuition first, then the estimator, then the identifying assumptions, and—most important—what breaks identification and how a reader can tell. Throughout, the running applications are the two domains where causal inference has reshaped marketing practice: advertising measurement and pricing.

The stakes are not academic. A decade of large-scale field experiments has shown that observational and even quasi-experimental estimates of advertising’s return can be off not by a few percent but by an order of magnitude, and sometimes carry the wrong sign (Lewis and Rao 2015; Gordon et al. 2019b). A marketing scientist who cannot distinguish a credible causal estimate from an incredible one is a liability to the firm. By the end of this chapter the reader will be able to state the estimand, choose a design, defend its assumptions, implement the estimator in R, and diagnose the most common failures.

44.1 Semester arc

This chapter is organized as a fourteen-week doctoral seminar in causal inference and field experiments, tuned to quantitative-marketing applications—advertising measurement, pricing, promotions, and digital/platform experimentation. The arc matches how the topic is taught in the empirical track of top programs (MIT, Chicago Booth, Stanford GSB, Berkeley, Wharton, Columbia, Kellogg, NYU Stern, and the economics and statistics departments marketing students cross-register into). The single organizing question is what makes the treatment as-good-as-randomly assigned, conditional on what we observe and how we designed the study?

The first third establishes the framework (potential outcomes and the assignment mechanism), the gold standard (randomized experiments and large-scale A/B testing), and the realistic case where randomization is absent (selection on observables, and why regression is not magic). The ordering is deliberate: students internalize the experimental ideal before judging how far an observational design falls short of it. The middle third is a tour of quasi-experimental designs, each motivated by a different source of as-good-as-random variation: instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, synthetic control, panel/event-study methods, and matching/weighting. A recurring theme is that the past decade re-litigated the workhorses—most dramatically the two-way fixed-effects DiD estimator, long the default, shown to be badly biased under staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects. The seminar treats this episode as the field’s central methodological cautionary tale: a method can be standard, published thousands of times, and still wrong. The final third turns to the machine-learning and marketing-platform frontier: ML for heterogeneous treatment effects; advertising measurement when effects are tiny relative to sales noise; the experimental designs platforms actually use (ghost ads, PSA holdouts, geo experiments); incrementality, pricing, and targeting-policy evaluation; and the interference/spillover problems that break SUTVA in marketplaces and social networks. The course closes on the question every marketing dissertation must answer: given that the effect is real but small and the platform is non-stationary, what is the credible research design, and can it scale?

The standing textbooks for the whole course are Imbens and Rubin’s Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences (Cambridge, 2015, the potential-outcomes spine), Angrist and Pischke’s Mostly Harmless Econometrics (Princeton, 2009, the applied quasi-experimental workhorse), Cunningham’s Causal Inference: The Mixtape (Yale, 2021, a modern code-forward synthesis), and Wooldridge’s Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data, 2nd ed. (MIT, 2010, the panel/fixed-effects reference). Each weekly module below names its topic, subtopics, methods, key readings (with DOI links and a one-line rationale; foundational works are marked [F], frontier works [R]), and central debate. The detailed derivations, R simulations, and worked marketing examples that follow the weekly map—the potential-outcomes algebra, the A/B-power simulation, the DiD/IV/RD/SCM code, and the design-comparison table—are the seminar’s lab sessions; they are kept intact and cross-referenced from the weeks they support.

44.1.1 Week 1 — Potential Outcomes and the Assignment Mechanism

Topic. [F] The Neyman–Rubin potential-outcomes model as the language in which a causal effect is defined before any estimator is chosen.

Subtopics. The fundamental problem of causal inference; SUTVA; the estimands (ATE, ATT, CATE); the assignment mechanism as the central object; “no causation without manipulation”; causal versus predictive questions.

Methods. Writing an estimand precisely; distinguishing estimand / identification / estimation / inference; recognizing when a question is causal versus descriptive. Worked algebra in Section 44.2 below.

Key readings.

  • Rubin, D. B. (1974). “Estimating Causal Effects of Treatments in Randomized and Nonrandomized Studies.” Journal of Educational Psychology 66(5), 688–701. doi:10.1037/h0037350 — [F] the founding statement of the potential-outcomes framework.
  • Holland, P. W. (1986). “Statistics and Causal Inference.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 81(396), 945–960. doi:10.1080/01621459.1986.10478354 — [F] formalizes the framework and the “no causation without manipulation” doctrine; the field’s conceptual touchstone.
  • Imbens, G. W. & Rubin, D. B. (2015). Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences, Part I. Cambridge University Press (book) — [F] potential outcomes and the assignment mechanism, in book length.

Debate. Is “manipulation” required for causality (what of immutable characteristics)? ATE versus ATT versus policy-relevant estimands; design-based versus model-based inference.

Controversy: the fast-food study that made design-based inference respectable

Marketing’s causal-inference toolkit is borrowed almost entirely from economics, and it was forged in a public argument worth knowing, because the moves both sides made are the moves a referee will make about your identification strategy.

1994 — the natural experiment. Card and Krueger study employment at fast-food restaurants either side of the New Jersey–Pennsylvania border after New Jersey raised its minimum wage, and report no employment loss—against a strong theoretical prior that it should fall.1 The design is the point: a policy boundary supplies the comparison, rather than a functional form.

2000 — the data are attacked, not the logic. Neumark and Wascher (2000) reanalyze the question using payroll records rather than the original telephone survey, and report results pointing the other way. The critique is aimed squarely at measurement: if your outcome is self-reported employment collected by phone, your finding is only as good as that instrument.

2000 — the reply, same issue. Card and Krueger (2000) respond with a further data source and maintain the original conclusion, while conceding what the payroll data do and do not show.

Why it belongs in this chapter. Notice where the argument went. Nobody disputed that a border discontinuity, if the data are sound, identifies something interpretable. The fight moved immediately to measurement—which is where design-based disputes almost always end up once the design itself is credible. That is the standard your own difference-in-differences will be held to (Section 44.1.5): a referee who accepts your design will then ask where your outcome variable came from, and “the platform’s dashboard” is an answer with the same structure as “a telephone survey.”

44.1.2 Week 2 — Randomized Experiments and A/B Testing at Scale

Topic. [F]→[R] Randomization as the assignment mechanism that identifies the ATE, scaled up to industrial web experimentation.

Subtopics. Fisher’s sharp null and randomization inference versus Neyman’s repeated-sampling inference; covariate balance, stratification, and blocking; CUPED-style variance reduction; the engineering of web experimentation, sample-ratio mismatch, peeking/optional stopping, and the experimentation platform as an organizational artifact.

Methods. Running Fisherian permutation tests; computing Neyman variance; designing stratified/clustered assignment; variance reduction; diagnosing sample-ratio mismatch. Lab: the A/B-power simulation in Section 44.3 below (Figure 44.3).

Key readings.

  • Kohavi, R., Longbotham, R., Sommerfield, D. & Henne, R. M. (2009). “Controlled Experiments on the Web: Survey and Practical Guide.” Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 18(1), 140–181. doi:10.1007/s10618-008-0114-1 — [R] the practitioner canon for industrial-scale A/B testing; the pitfalls students will actually hit.
  • Bojinov, I. & Shephard, N. (2019). “Time Series Experiments and Causal Estimands: Exact Randomization Tests and Trading.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 114(528), 1665–1682. doi:10.1080/01621459.2018.1527225 — [R] extends design-based randomization inference to single-unit, switchback-style time-series experiments (directly relevant to one-market pricing/ad tests).
  • Imbens, G. W. & Rubin, D. B. (2015). Causal Inference…, Part II. Cambridge University Press (book) — [F] classical randomized experiments; Fisher and Neyman inference.
  • Huch, E., Nail, S. A., Melconian, T., Vongsathorn, X. & Feinberg, F. (2026). “Overall Evaluation Criteria for A/B Tests: A Meta-Analytic Approach.” Marketing Science, published online ahead of print. doi:10.1287/mksc.2025.0164 — [R] pools an archive of experiments to estimate each test’s long-run effect from short-run metrics; method and replication in Section 44.4.

Debate. Fisher versus Neyman inference; fixed-horizon versus sequential/always-valid testing; how much can web A/B testing actually learn given non-stationarity and short windows?

44.1.3 Week 3 — Regression and Selection on Observables

Topic. [F] The conditional-independence (unconfoundedness) assumption and what regression actually estimates under it.

Subtopics. Regression as a weighting/comparison estimator and what it estimates under heterogeneity; “bad controls” and collider bias; the overlap/common-support condition; omitted-variable bias and sensitivity.

Methods. Specifying a credible conditioning set; drawing causal DAGs to spot bad controls and colliders; checking overlap; OVB sensitivity bounds. The selection-bias decomposition is derived in Section 44.2.1 below, and Section 44.10 works an Oster bound on published numbers.

Controversy: can matching recover an experimental answer?

This is the single most relevant economics dispute for anyone doing marketing attribution, because it is the same question in different clothes: when you have observational data and a conditioning set, can you recover what a randomized experiment would have found?

1986 — the benchmark, and the bad news. LaLonde takes a randomized job-training experiment, discards the experimental control group, substitutes non-experimental comparison groups drawn from survey data, and applies the econometric estimators of the day.2 They do not recover the experimental answer. The estimates vary widely with specification and comparison group, and an analyst without the experimental benchmark would have had no way to know which was right.

1999 — the optimistic reassessment. Dehejia and Wahba (1999) revisit the same data with propensity-score methods and report that, with careful matching and attention to overlap, the experimental estimate can be recovered. This result is enormously influential and is a large part of why propensity-score matching spread across the applied social sciences.

2005 — the qualification. Smith and Todd (2005) ask, in their title, Does Matching Overcome LaLonde’s Critique of Nonexperimental Estimators? Their answer is: not robustly. The favorable results are sensitive to the particular sample and specification choices, and the performance degrades when those choices vary.

What survives, and what it means for attribution. The defensible reading is that matching helps when the comparison group is drawn from the same population, faces the same environment, and is compared on rich pre-treatment covariates including the outcome’s own history—and is unreliable otherwise. Notice that this is the same conclusion the advertising literature reached independently (Chapter 14): observational methods benchmarked against experiments diverge, and not with a constant bias one could correct. Two literatures, thirty years apart, arriving at the same place is worth more than either alone.

Key readings.

  • Athey, S. & Imbens, G. W. (2017). “The State of Applied Econometrics: Causality and Policy Evaluation.” Journal of Economic Perspectives 31(2), 3–32. doi:10.1257/jep.31.2.3 — [R] the modern map of identification strategies and where selection-on-observables sits among them; assigned as the course’s strategic overview.
  • Angrist, J. D. & Pischke, J.-S. (2009). Mostly Harmless Econometrics, ch. 3. Princeton University Press (book) — [F] regression and the conditional-independence assumption; the “bad control” problem.
  • Imbens, G. W. & Rubin, D. B. (2015). Causal Inference…, Part III. Cambridge University Press (book) — [F] unconfoundedness and regression.

Debate. When is “control for everything” self-defeating? How much faith can selection-on-observables ever earn without a design?

44.1.4 Week 4 — Instrumental Variables

Topic. [F] Recovering causal effects from an exogenous shifter of an endogenous treatment.

Subtopics. The IV/2SLS estimator; the LATE theorem and the monotonicity/exclusion/relevance assumptions; compliers and what LATE is the effect for; weak instruments; judge/examiner and shift-share designs; IV in marketing (price endogeneity, demand estimation).

Methods. 2SLS and its LATE interpretation; first-stage F / weak-IV diagnostics; reasoning about exclusion and monotonicity in a real application. Lab: the demand-estimation IV simulation in Section 44.6 below.

Key readings.

  • Imbens, G. W. & Angrist, J. D. (1994). “Identification and Estimation of Local Average Treatment Effects.” Econometrica 62(2), 467–475. doi:10.2307/2951620 — [F] the LATE theorem; redefines what IV identifies under heterogeneity.
  • Angrist, J. D., Imbens, G. W. & Rubin, D. B. (1996). “Identification of Causal Effects Using Instrumental Variables.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 91(434), 444–455. doi:10.1080/01621459.1996.10476902 — [F] embeds IV in potential outcomes; the canonical compliers/defiers exposition.
  • Angrist, J. D. & Pischke, J.-S. (2009). Mostly Harmless Econometrics, ch. 4. Princeton University Press (book) — [F] applied IV and weak-instrument diagnostics.

Debate. Is LATE a “policy-relevant” estimand or an artifact of the instrument? Are most instruments’ exclusion restrictions defensible?

44.1.5 Week 5 — Difference-in-Differences I: Foundations and the 2×2

Topic. [F] The canonical 2×2 DiD and the parallel-trends assumption.

Subtopics. Event-study/pre-trend plots; clustered and serially correlated standard errors; placebo and pre-trend tests; DiD for marketing launches, entry, and policy/regulatory shocks.

Methods. Building event-study plots; testing parallel pre-trends; clustering and wild-cluster bootstrap; placebo tests. Lab: the DiD panel simulation in Section 44.5 below.

Key readings.

  • Bertrand, M., Duflo, E. & Mullainathan, S. (2004). “How Much Should We Trust Differences-in-Differences Estimates?” The Quarterly Journal of Economics 119(1), 249–275. doi:10.1162/003355304772839588 — [F] exposes serial-correlation underestimation of DiD standard errors; the inference cautionary tale.
  • Card, D. & Krueger, A. B. (2000). “Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania: Reply.” American Economic Review 90(5), 1397–1420. doi:10.1257/aer.90.5.1397 — [F] the verified record for the canonical minimum-wage DiD program; the design that made DiD a default tool. (The original Card & Krueger 1994 AER article is (DOI to verify).)
  • Angrist, J. D. & Pischke, J.-S. (2009). Mostly Harmless Econometrics, ch. 5. Princeton University Press (book) — [F] DiD and fixed effects, the classical treatment.

Debate. Is parallel trends testable, or only falsifiable on pre-periods? How much should inference (not point estimates) drive DiD credibility?

44.1.6 Week 6 — Difference-in-Differences II: Staggered Adoption and the TWFE Critique

Topic. [R] The field’s central recent methodological episode: why two-way fixed-effects DiD is biased under staggered timing and heterogeneous effects, and the family of robust estimators that replaced it.

Subtopics. “Forbidden comparisons” and negative weights; decomposition diagnostics; the new robust estimators (group-time ATTs, interaction-weighted event studies, imputation); choosing among them; honest pre-trends.

Methods. Running Goodman-Bacon decompositions; estimating the Callaway–Sant’Anna, Sun–Abraham, and Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess estimators and reconciling them; honest pre-trend (HonestDiD-style) sensitivity. The TWFE failure is introduced in the DiD discussion at Section 44.5.

Key readings.

  • Goodman-Bacon, A. (2021). “Difference-in-Differences with Variation in Treatment Timing.” Journal of Econometrics 225(2), 254–277. doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2021.03.014 — [R] the decomposition showing TWFE is a weighted average of all 2×2s, including “forbidden” already-treated comparisons.

  • de Chaisemartin, C. & d’Haultfœuille, X. (2020). “Two-Way Fixed Effects Estimators with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects.” American Economic Review 110(9), 2964–2996. doi:10.1257/aer.20181169 — [R] proves TWFE can put negative weights on treatment effects; offers a robust alternative.

  • Callaway, B. & Sant’Anna, P. H. C. (2021). “Difference-in-Differences with Multiple Time Periods.” Journal of Econometrics 225(2), 200–230. doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.12.001 — [R] the group-time ATT estimator that is now a default robust DiD.

  • Sun, L. & Abraham, S. (2021). “Estimating Dynamic Treatment Effects in Event Studies with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects.” Journal of Econometrics 225(2), 175–199. doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2020.09.006 — [R] fixes contamination of event-study coefficients; the interaction-weighted estimator.

  • Borusyak, K., Jaravel, X. & Spiess, J. (2024). “Revisiting Event-Study Designs: Robust and Efficient Estimation.” Review of Economic Studies 92(5), 3253–3285. doi:10.1093/restud/rdae007 — [R] the imputation (efficient) estimator and a unifying view of event-study designs.

  • Roth, J., Sant’Anna, P. H. C., Bilinski, A. & Poe, J. (2023). “What’s Trending in Difference-in-Differences? A Synthesis of the Recent Econometrics Literature.” Journal of Econometrics 235(2), 2218–2244. doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2023.03.008 — [R] the synthesis/decision guide assigned as the week’s anchor.

  • Liu, Q., Jiang, S., Qiu, L. & Huo, B. (2026). “Platform Competition and Adoption Heterogeneity: How Dockless Bike Sharing Shapes Urban Air Quality.” Production and Operations Management. doi:10.1177/10591478261472202 — [F] an applied stacked-DiD design over a staggered two-firm rollout, in which the average effect is entirely driven by one market structure (worked through at Section 70.7.1).

  • Chan, K. W., Wetzel, H. A., Pupovac, L., Dekimpe, M. G. & Loske, D. (2026). “EV Charging Availability and Grocery Store Performance.” Journal of Marketing Research. doi:10.1177/00222437261491290 — [F] Callaway–Sant’Anna estimates for chargers that reached 42 of 332 supermarkets in different months, after a Goodman-Bacon decomposition finds a 10% negative-weighting bias in two-way fixed effects; the robustness ladder (late adopters as controls, stacked synthetic-control DiD, catchment radii for SUTVA) is worked through at

    Section 54.6.1.

  • Luca, M., Nagaraj, A. & Subramani, G. (2026). “Getting on the Map: The Impact of Online Listings on Business Performance.” Management Science 72(10), 9199–9214. doi:10.1287/mnsc.2024.04716 — [F] Gardner’s two-stage imputation estimator on an unbalanced establishment panel of public tax receipts. Two-way fixed effects give about half the two-stage estimate in the bulk-import sample. Section 33.8 re-runs the design on the public data with planted listing dates, to show which threats the estimator handles and which it cannot.

Debate. Which robust estimator, when? Is the efficient imputation estimator’s stronger modeling worth it? How much published DiD work is invalidated? When a staggered rollout involves two competing entrants, is the estimand of interest the effect of entry, or the effect of the market structure that entry produces?

44.1.7 Week 7 — Regression Discontinuity Designs

Topic. [F]→[R] Identifying the local effect at a known assignment threshold, with modern robust inference.

Subtopics. Sharp and fuzzy RDD; continuity-based versus local-randomization views; bandwidth/kernel choice and the bias–variance tradeoff; manipulation/sorting tests (density discontinuity); RDD in marketing (loyalty-tier thresholds, ad-auction reserve prices, eligibility cutoffs).

Methods. Local-polynomial estimation; MSE-optimal and CER-optimal bandwidths; density (McCrary-style) manipulation tests; placebo cutoffs. Lab: the loyalty-tier RD simulation in Section 44.7 below (Figure 44.11).

Key readings.

  • Imbens, G. W. & Lemieux, T. (2008). “Regression Discontinuity Designs: A Guide to Practice.” Journal of Econometrics 142(2), 615–635. doi:10.1016/j.jeconom.2007.05.001 — [F] the practitioner’s guide that standardized RDD practice.
  • Calonico, S., Cattaneo, M. D. & Titiunik, R. (2014). “Robust Nonparametric Confidence Intervals for Regression-Discontinuity Designs.” Econometrica 82(6), 2295–2326. doi:10.3982/ecta11757 — [R] robust bias-corrected inference and data-driven bandwidths; the modern default.
  • Liu, S., Zhang, F., Wang, J. & Gao, B. 44.2 The Potential-Outcomes Framework

The foundational move of modern causal inference is to define the effect of a treatment for each unit before worrying about how to estimate it. Following the Neyman–Rubin potential-outcomes model, let \(D_i \in \{0,1\}\) denote whether unit \(i\) (a consumer, a store, a geographic market, a designated market area) receives a treatment—an ad campaign, a price cut, a new feature. Associate with each unit two potential outcomes: \(Y_i(1)\), the outcome that would occur under treatment, and \(Y_i(0)\), the outcome that would occur under control. The unit-level treatment effect is their difference,

\[ \tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0). \tag{44.1}\]

The defining difficulty—the fundamental problem of causal inference—is that for any unit we observe only one potential outcome. The realized outcome is

\[ Y_i = D_i\,Y_i(1) + (1 - D_i)\,Y_i(0), \tag{44.2}\]

so the other potential outcome is a counterfactual that is missing by construction. We never see \(\tau_i\) for any single unit. Causal inference is therefore, at root, a missing-data problem, and progress comes from estimating averages of \(\tau_i\) over populations rather than the unit-level effects themselves.

A causal effect is a comparison of two states of the world that differ only in the treatment: the outcome we observe under the treatment a unit received, and the outcome that same unit would have realized under the treatment it did not receive. Because only one of these is ever observed, every causal estimate rests on an assumption that makes the missing outcome recoverable from the data.

The chief estimand is the average treatment effect (ATE), \(\tau_{\text{ATE}} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]\), the expected effect of moving a randomly chosen unit from control to treatment. Two relatives matter in practice. The average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), \(\tau_{\text{ATT}} = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1]\), is the effect for the units that actually received treatment—the relevant quantity when asking whether a campaign that ran paid off. The conditional average treatment effect (CATE), \(\tau(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0) \mid \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]\), is the effect for a subpopulation with covariates \(\mathbf{x}\), the target of modern heterogeneous-treatment-effect and targeting methods.3

44.2.1 Why the Naive Comparison Fails

The intuitive estimator of a treatment effect is the difference in mean outcomes between treated and untreated units, \(\hat\Delta = \bar Y_{D=1} - \bar Y_{D=0}\). Decomposing its probability limit exposes exactly why it is biased. Adding and subtracting \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1]\) gives

\[ \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid D_i = 0]}_{\text{naive difference}} = \underbrace{\tau_{\text{ATT}}}_{\text{causal effect}} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]}_{\text{selection bias}}. \tag{44.3}\]

The second term is selection bias: the difference in the baseline (untreated) outcome between the groups that did and did not get treated. It is zero only if treated and untreated units would have looked the same absent treatment. In marketing they almost never do. A firm targets ads at consumers already inclined to buy; it cuts prices on products whose demand is already softening; loyal customers self-select into a rewards program. In each case \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] \neq \mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]\), and the naive difference confounds the effect of the treatment with the reasons the unit was treated. The remainder of this chapter is a catalogue of designs that drive the selection-bias term to zero—by randomization, or by an assumption that makes the untreated a valid stand-in for the treated counterfactual.

Two assumptions are maintained throughout unless stated otherwise. SUTVA (the stable-unit-treatment-value assumption) requires that one unit’s potential outcomes not depend on other units’ treatment assignments (no interference) and that there be a single version of the treatment. SUTVA is violated by spillovers—a price promotion at one store cannibalizing a neighbor, an ad shown to one household influencing another through word of mouth—which is why experimental units in marketing are often geographies rather than individuals. Overlap (positivity) requires \(0 < \Pr(D_i = 1 \mid \mathbf{X}_i) < 1\) for all covariate values, so that comparable treated and control units exist at every \(\mathbf{x}\). Overlap is often treated as the easy half of strong ignorability, but algorithmic allocation can violate it by design. An ad auction that always awards an impression to the top bidder gives many users a propensity of exactly zero or one. DML and inverse-propensity weighting then recover the effect only for users whose assignment was genuinely random, even though the logged allocation rule makes assignment unconfounded (Rafieian 2026) (see Section 14.5).

Figure 44.1 situates the designs of this chapter on a spectrum from the strongest identification (randomization, where assumptions hold by construction) to designs that buy identification with progressively stronger, untestable assumptions.

44.3 Randomized Experiments and A/B Tests

Randomization is the gold standard because it eliminates selection bias by construction rather than by assumption. If treatment \(D_i\) is assigned independently of the potential outcomes—\(\{Y_i(0), Y_i(1)\} \perp D_i\)—then the untreated group is, in expectation, a valid counterfactual for the treated group: \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]\). The selection-bias term in Equation 44.3 vanishes, and the difference in means is unbiased for the ATE,

\[ \hat\tau_{\text{ATE}} = \bar Y_{D=1} - \bar Y_{D=0}. \tag{44.4}\]

The identifying assumption—independence of assignment and potential outcomes—holds because the experimenter, not the units, controls \(D_i\). This is the single most important idea in the chapter: randomization does not make treated and control units identical, it makes them exchangeable in expectation, which is all that Equation 44.4 requires.

In the digital economy this logic is operationalized at enormous scale as the A/B test (online controlled experiment): users arriving at a site are randomly bucketed into a control arm seeing the incumbent experience and one or more treatment arms seeing a variant, and a metric—conversion, revenue per session, retention—is compared across arms. The mechanics are simple; the discipline is in the design. Three issues dominate practice.

Power and the minimum detectable effect. An experiment that cannot detect the effect sizes that matter is worse than no experiment, because it invites the fallacy of accepting the null. For a two-arm test of a mean with equal allocation, the sample size per arm needed to detect a true difference \(\delta\) at significance level \(\alpha\) and power \(1-\beta\) is approximately

\[ n \;\approx\; \frac{2\,(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2\,\sigma^2}{\delta^2}, \tag{44.5}\]

where \(\sigma^2\) is the outcome variance and \(z_p\) the standard-normal quantile. The quadratic dependence on \(\delta\) is the crux of advertising measurement: sales are so volatile relative to advertising’s effect that the required sample is often larger than even large firms can muster, a point developed below.

The randomization unit and interference. When treating a user can affect other users—social spillovers, marketplace competition for the same inventory, supply constraints—unit-level randomization violates SUTVA and biases the estimate. Cluster-randomizing at the level of the interference (markets, regions, social clusters) restores validity at the cost of effective sample size.

Peeking and the validity of the stopping rule. Repeatedly testing a running experiment and stopping the first time \(p < 0.05\) inflates the false-positive rate far above the nominal level. Either fix the sample size in advance, or adopt a sequential procedure (always-valid \(p\)-values, group-sequential boundaries) whose error guarantee survives continuous monitoring.

The following simulation makes the bias-then-fix logic concrete: it first shows that a confounded observational comparison recovers the wrong effect, then that randomization recovers the truth. Figure 44.2 diagrams the two assignment mechanisms the simulation contrasts.

Code
set.seed(47)

# Data-generating process: a latent 'propensity' drives BOTH self-selection
# into treatment (observationally) AND the baseline outcome -> confounding.
make_population <- function(n, true_tau = 0.20) {
  propensity <- rnorm(n)                       # latent buying inclination
  Y0 <- 0.50 + 0.40 * propensity + rnorm(n)    # untreated potential outcome
  Y1 <- Y0 + true_tau                          # constant treatment effect
  data.frame(propensity, Y0, Y1)
}

# (1) OBSERVATIONAL: high-propensity users self-select into treatment.
n <- 4000
pop <- make_population(n)
D_obs <- as.integer(pop$propensity + rnorm(n) > 0)   # selection on propensity
Y_obs <- ifelse(D_obs == 1, pop$Y1, pop$Y0)
naive <- mean(Y_obs[D_obs == 1]) - mean(Y_obs[D_obs == 0])

# (2) RANDOMIZED: assignment independent of potential outcomes.
rct_estimate <- function(n_per_arm = 1000, true_tau = 0.20) {
  p <- make_population(2 * n_per_arm, true_tau)
  D <- rep(0:1, each = n_per_arm)
  D <- sample(D)                               # random assignment
  Y <- ifelse(D == 1, p$Y1, p$Y0)
  mean(Y[D == 1]) - mean(Y[D == 0])
}
rct_draws <- replicate(2000, rct_estimate())

cat(sprintf("True effect (ATE):              %.3f\n", 0.20))
#> True effect (ATE):              0.200
cat(sprintf("Naive observational estimate:   %.3f  (biased)\n", naive))
#> Naive observational estimate:   0.737  (biased)
cat(sprintf("Mean of randomized estimates:   %.3f  (unbiased)\n", mean(rct_draws)))
#> Mean of randomized estimates:   0.201  (unbiased)

hist(rct_draws, breaks = 40, col = "grey80", border = "white",
     main = "", xlab = "Estimated treatment effect")
abline(v = 0.20, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = naive, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
legend("topright", bty = "n",
       legend = c("true effect (0.20)", "naive observational"),
       lwd = 2, lty = c(2, 1), col = c("black", "firebrick"))

44.3.1 Advertising Measurement: The Hard Case for Experiments

Advertising is the canonical setting where experiments are both essential and difficult. The difficulty is statistical, and Equation 44.5 explains it. The effect of a typical online display campaign on purchase probability is small in absolute terms, while individual purchasing is enormously variable; substituting realistic magnitudes into Equation 44.5 implies that detecting advertising’s true return on investment with confidence can require millions of randomized users—more than many campaigns ever reach (Lewis and Rao 2015). Lewis and Rao show that even well-powered experiments deliver confidence intervals on ROI so wide that firms cannot distinguish a profitable campaign from a money-losing one, and that the observational regressions firms typically run fare far worse.

How much worse is documented by large-scale comparisons. Across digital advertising experiments at scale, observational methods—matching, regression adjustment, propensity scores—routinely yield estimates that diverge sharply from the experimental benchmark, frequently overstating effects by large multiples and occasionally reversing their sign, because no set of observed covariates fully captures why a platform showed a given user a given ad (Gordon et al. 2019b). The lesson is not that observational methods are useless but that, in advertising, the selection-bias term in Equation 44.3 is large relative to the effect itself, so even small failures of the conditional-independence assumption swamp the signal. A recurrent culprit is activity bias: users who are online and active are both more likely to be served (and to “see”) an ad and more likely to convert for reasons unrelated to the ad, manufacturing a spurious correlation that intention-to-treat experimental designs avoid (Lewis, Rao, and Reiley 2011).

These findings reframe the practitioner’s task. The question is rarely “what is the point estimate of ROI?” but “is my experiment powered to answer the decision I face?”—and often the honest answer is to redesign the test (larger, geo-based, or focused on an intermediate outcome) rather than to trust an underpowered or observational number.

A constructive answer to the scaling problem treats each experiment as one labelled observation rather than as a one-off verdict. Gordon, Moakler, and Zettelmeyer (2026) train a model on 2,226 Meta experiments to predict a campaign’s incremental conversions per dollar from campaign aggregates (the test group’s conversion rate, its exposure rate, last-click counts) and apply it to campaigns run without a control group. The features would be bad controls in a user-level causal model, because they are outcomes of the campaign; in a campaign-level prediction model they are legitimate, because the experiments, not the features, carry the identification. The distinction between identifying an effect and predicting one that has already been identified elsewhere is developed, with a replication of the paper’s simulations, in Section 14.4.

44.3.2 Born or Made? Field Data Plus a Randomized Experience Manipulation

Advertising is the case where the selection term in Equation 44.3 swamps the effect. A common marketing variant is subtler: the treatment is an experience the customer chooses, and the question is whether the experience changes later behavior or merely reveals who the customer already was. Kim et al. (2026) pose exactly this question about product customization. In a retailer’s transaction records, customers who customize once are more likely to customize again, and they spend more, visit more often, and buy more items. Write \(D_i = 1\) for “customized at least once” and \(Y_i\) for later customization or spend. The naive contrast then adds the causal effect of the experience to a selection term, \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid D_i = 0]\), which is the difference in later behavior that an inherent taste for customizing would produce even without the experience. Transaction data alone cannot separate “born” customizers from “made” ones.

The paper’s multimethod answer, sketched in Figure 44.4, adds longitudinal experiments that randomize the experience itself. Some participants are assigned to customize and others to choose from a matched set of ready-made products, and later choices are tracked. The matched set is the design detail that matters. Comparing customization with a generic or worse product would mix the effect of the customizing experience with the effect of getting a better-fitting product. Matching the choice set keeps the comparison on the experience. Because assignment is random, the inherent preference is balanced across arms in expectation (the dashed path in the figure no longer reaches treatment), and the difference in later customization identifies the effect of the experience. The authors find that an initial customization experience significantly raises the subsequent likelihood of customizing, with favorable downstream outcomes for customer and retailer, so at least part of the field correlation is a causal journey effect rather than pure sorting.

The design also shows what each half of the evidence buys. The field data supply external validity: real customers, real money, and a nine-year horizon long enough to see repeat behavior. They are weak on identification. The experiments supply identification and are weaker on external validity, because the participants, products, and stakes are the experimenters’ rather than the retailer’s. Neither half alone gives the quantity a retailer most wants, which is how much of the observed customizer premium would appear among customers who customize only because the firm nudged them. That is the question Section 16.8.2 takes up, and the answer depends on how closely the experimental experience matches the field intervention. (Only the published abstract was accessible when this section was written. It does not report the field sample size, how the transaction analysis adjusts for self-selection, or the number and sizes of the experiments, so this description stays at the level of the design logic.)

44.3.3 Policy Lotteries and the Estimand You Actually Want

Not every randomization is run by a researcher. Governments allocate scarce rights by lottery—visas, permits, school seats, subsidy slots—and those lotteries are experiments whose treatment is a policy, which is often the treatment a decision-maker cares about and rarely the one a study estimates. Clemens and Lewis (2026) make the distinction sharply. The dominant identification strategy in their literature instruments for immigrant presence with historical settlement patterns, which identifies a local average treatment effect of varying immigrant supply regardless of current demand. The policy question is different: what happens when a quota binds on firms that want to hire now? That is a policy-relevant treatment effect, and it is recovered by the quota’s own randomization—the H-2B visa lottery—rather than by an instrument built from history.

Three features of the design are worth importing into marketing work whenever an allocation rule contains randomness. The randomization is at the level of the decision-making unit (the firm), not the individual, so the estimates speak to firm-level adjustment rather than to worker-level exposure. Hypotheses, subsample tests, and predicted signs were committed to a pre-analysis plan before data collection, which converts the heterogeneity analysis from exploration into a test. And the outcome data come from a purpose-built survey of winners and losers rather than from whatever administrative file happened to exist, with prespecified checks on item and global nonresponse. Marketing has more of these opportunities than it uses: oversubscribed beta programs, capacity-rationed loyalty perks, lotteried event invitations, and regulator-run license allocations all embed randomization that a firm can exploit without running an experiment of its own. Section 76.5 treats the same paper as a template for writing up a mechanism rather than an average.

The same logic applies when the randomized policy is an enforcement action rather than an allocation. Fan, Guo, and Ke (2026) use China’s randomized pre-IPO on-site inspection program, under which the securities regulator draws a random subset of IPO applicants for intensive inspection of their books, to estimate the causal effect of proactive public enforcement on the financial reporting quality of applicants in a setting with weak institutional oversight. Selected applicants end up with better reporting, largely because inspection screens out firms with questionable disclosures. The larger effect is deterrence: later applicants, who were never drawn, submit higher-quality reports because they might be. The cost is that some firms that would have merited approval are rejected. Two features carry over to marketing settings. Randomizing the point of enforcement identifies the policy-relevant effect of scrutiny itself, free of the targeting that makes ordinary audits uninformative about deterrence, and the deterrence result is a spillover onto untreated units of exactly the kind Chapter 71 warns will contaminate a naive comparison of inspected firms with their uninspected peers. (Only the published abstract was accessible when this section was written; the magnitudes are in the paper.)

Firms run policy experiments too, and the same point about estimands applies. Fang et al. (2026) randomized nearly one million customers of a global e-commerce platform between an AI-decided, returnless partial refund and the standard process of shipping the item back for a full refund. The treatment arm changes three things at once: who decides, whether the item comes back, and how much is refunded. The experiment therefore identifies the effect of the policy as it would be deployed, not the effect of any single component, and the deployment effect is the quantity the platform’s decision turns on. The outcomes are chosen the same way. Refund payouts, processing costs, later purchasing, and strategic claiming each enter the platform’s payoff, and the paper reports all of them rather than a single headline metric (Section 76.5).

44.4 Overall Evaluation Criteria: Learning Across A/B Tests

A single A/B test answers a narrow question well: did this variant move this metric over these two weeks? The decision the firm faces is wider. It wants to know whether the variant raises long-run value, and the metrics that measure long-run value (six-month revenue, retention, closed transactions) are slow and noisy, while the metrics that are fast and precise (clicks, form fills, sessions) are only proxies. Practitioners resolve the tension with an overall evaluation criterion (OEC): one number, built from short-run metrics, that is supposed to track long-run value (Kohavi, Tang, and Xu 2020). In most firms the OEC is a weighted sum whose weights were negotiated in a meeting.

Huch et al. (2026) replace the meeting with a model. Their observation is that a firm that has run hundreds of experiments already owns the data needed to learn how short-run effects map to long-run effects: every past test whose long-run outcome has matured is one observation on that mapping. The method is a multivariate random-effects meta-analysis, the tool biostatisticians built to validate surrogate endpoints in clinical trials (DerSimonian and Laird 1986; Buyse et al. 2000), applied to an archive of A/B tests. It needs only two summaries per test, a vector of effect estimates and its covariance matrix, and it returns for every test, finished or still running, a posterior distribution for the long-run effect. This section sets out the full method, reports what the authors find in 190 tests at Zillow, and replicates the estimators in R.

44.4.1 Setup: what the archive must contain

Index past experiments by \(t = 1, \dots, T\). Each test reports a vector of estimated treatment effects on \(p\) metrics, \(\mathbf z_t \in \mathbb R^p\), together with an estimate of its sampling covariance \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_t\). With a difference in means, \(\mathbf z_t = \bar{\mathbf m}_{t1} - \bar{\mathbf m}_{t0}\) and \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_t = \mathbf S_{t1}/n_{t1} + \mathbf S_{t0}/n_{t0}\), where \(\mathbf S_{ta}\) is the sample covariance matrix of the metrics in arm \(a\). Any estimator will do, including a covariate-adjusted one such as CUPED (Deng et al. 2013), as long as two conditions hold. The estimate must be approximately Gaussian around the true effect vector \(\boldsymbol\mu_t\), and the covariance estimate must be consistent, so that it can be treated as known:

\[ \mathbf z_t \mid \boldsymbol\mu_t \;\sim\; \mathcal N\!\left(\boldsymbol\mu_t, \boldsymbol\Sigma_t\right). \tag{44.6}\]

The only new bookkeeping relative to standard practice is the off-diagonal part of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_t\). A platform that analyzes one metric at a time already computes the diagonal; the method also needs the covariances between metrics, and it needs metric definitions and measurement windows that are the same across tests. In the Zillow application these summaries shrink the data from billions of customer-level rows to a few hundred.

Split the metrics into two groups, \(\mathbf z_t = (\mathbf y_t^\top, \mathbf x_t^\top)^\top\), with true effects \(\boldsymbol\mu_t = (\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}^\top, \boldsymbol\mu_{xt}^\top)^\top\). The \(r\) metrics in \(\mathbf y_t\) are the key performance indicators the business cares about. The \(q\) metrics in \(\mathbf x_t\) are proxies. Both are estimated effects on post-treatment outcomes; neither is a covariate. The analyst then defines the target as a function of the true KPI effects,

\[ \text{OEC}_t \;=\; f\!\left(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}\right), \tag{44.7}\]

and the three examples in the paper cover most uses. With one KPI, such as revenue per customer over six months, \(f\) is the identity. With revenue split by line of business, \(f(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}) = \mathbf 1_r^\top \boldsymbol\mu_{yt}\) adds the lines up. With a conversion funnel whose stage-\(j\) effect is a log ratio of conditional conversion rates, \(f(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}) = \exp(\mathbf 1_r^\top \boldsymbol\mu_{yt}) - 1\) is the lift at the bottom of the funnel. The funnel case shows that the proxies need not be measured earlier than the KPI. Bottom-of-funnel events are rare, so their effects are estimated imprecisely even when the window is the same, and the upper-funnel metrics lend them precision.

Defining the OEC as a function of true effects is the step that separates this framework from an OEC by committee. The target is stated in business terms and never changes. What the model learns is how much each proxy says about it.

44.4.2 The benchmark: one test at a time

The estimator every platform already computes is the plug-in

\[ \widehat{\text{OEC}}_t = f(\mathbf y_t), \qquad \frac{\widehat{\text{OEC}}_t - \text{OEC}_t} {\sqrt{f'(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt})^\top \boldsymbol\Sigma_{yyt}\, f'(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt})}} \;\xrightarrow{d}\; \mathcal N(0, 1), \tag{44.8}\]

with the standard error from the delta method. The authors call it the naive method. It ignores the proxies and it ignores every other test. It is unbiased for each test taken alone, and it has two defects that matter in practice. Its intervals are wide, because the KPIs are noisy. And it is biased conditional on being selected: a firm ships the variants whose estimates are large and positive, and the estimates that clear that bar are disproportionately the ones whose noise happened to be positive. The summed “impact” of a year of shipped winners is therefore overstated, by regression to the mean.

44.4.3 The meta-analytic model

The fix is one added assumption. The true effect vectors of the tests in the archive are independent draws from a common distribution,

\[ \boldsymbol\mu_t \;\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\; P_{\boldsymbol\theta}, \qquad \boldsymbol\theta \sim p(\boldsymbol\theta \mid \boldsymbol\theta_0), \tag{44.9}\]

with a hyperprior on the unknown \(\boldsymbol\theta\). This is the standard exchangeability assumption of meta-analysis. Univariate versions were already in use for online experiments, for example to show that the distribution of true effects at Bing has fat tails (Azevedo et al. 2020). Because \(\boldsymbol\mu_t\) is a vector, \(P_{\boldsymbol\theta}\) carries more than a location and a spread: it carries the correlations between true effects on different metrics across experiments, and those correlations are what allow one metric to stand in for another. Figure 44.5 draws the model.

Why is the posterior the right estimator? Take squared-error loss and average it over both the sampling noise and the draw of \(\boldsymbol\mu_t\) from \(P_{\boldsymbol\theta}\). The estimator that minimizes this Bayes risk is the posterior mean of \(f(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt})\) given \(\mathbf z_t\). With \(\boldsymbol\theta\) unknown, the fully Bayesian version integrates over its posterior, and in practice that is done by applying \(f\) to Markov chain Monte Carlo draws of \(\boldsymbol\mu_{yt}\).

It helps to be exact about what has been assumed and what has not. Surrogate-index methods (Athey et al. 2026; Yang et al. 2024) work with individual-level data and assume that the long-run outcome is independent of treatment given the surrogates, so that the surrogates capture every channel through which treatment acts. The meta-analytic model makes no such claim about mechanisms. It replaces the causal surrogacy assumption with a statistical one about the population of experiments, and it measures the strength of surrogacy empirically, as a cross-experiment correlation, instead of assuming it. The cost is that Equation 44.9 must be credible. It is most credible for many closely related tests on one platform and one customer population. It fails when tests interfere with each other, when the archive mixes domains, or when something observable about a test predicts its effect. The authors’ remedy for the last case is metaregression: let the effect distribution depend on test-level covariates \(\mathbf w_t\) (platform, intervention type, duration, or summaries of \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_t\) if strong tests are stopped early) and require exchangeability only conditional on them. The assumption has observable consequences, so it can be checked with posterior predictive tests of dependence between \(\boldsymbol\mu_t\) and test metadata.

44.4.4 Three priors for the distribution of effects

Gaussian. With \(\boldsymbol\mu_t \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\eta, \boldsymbol\Omega)\), the posterior of a test’s true effects given \(\boldsymbol\theta = (\boldsymbol\eta, \boldsymbol\Omega)\) is available in closed form:

\[ \boldsymbol\mu_t \mid \mathbf z_t, \boldsymbol\theta \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\eta_t, \boldsymbol\Omega_t), \qquad \boldsymbol\Omega_t = \left(\boldsymbol\Omega^{-1} + \boldsymbol\Sigma_t^{-1}\right)^{-1}, \qquad \boldsymbol\eta_t = \boldsymbol\Omega_t\left(\boldsymbol\Omega^{-1}\boldsymbol\eta + \boldsymbol\Sigma_t^{-1}\mathbf z_t\right). \tag{44.10}\]

The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the archive’s mean effect and the test’s own estimate. It is the best linear unbiased predictor (BLUP) of \(\boldsymbol\mu_t\), which makes it the benchmark for any OEC that is linear in the metrics, including a committee’s weighted sum. Two properties follow from Equation 44.10. As a test grows, \(\boldsymbol\Sigma_t \to \mathbf 0\) and the BLUP converges to the naive estimate, so a large test is left alone. And because \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) has off-diagonal terms, a precise proxy estimate moves the posterior for a noisy KPI.

The second property gives the method its most practical use. Suppose only some metrics have been observed, \(\mathbf A \mathbf z_t\) for a selection matrix \(\mathbf A\), because the long-run window has not closed. The posterior becomes

\[ \boldsymbol\Omega_t = \left[\boldsymbol\Omega^{-1} + \mathbf A^\top\!\left(\mathbf A \boldsymbol\Sigma_t \mathbf A^\top\right)^{-1}\!\mathbf A\right]^{-1}, \qquad \boldsymbol\eta_t = \boldsymbol\Omega_t\left[\boldsymbol\Omega^{-1}\boldsymbol\eta + \mathbf A^\top\!\left(\mathbf A \boldsymbol\Sigma_t \mathbf A^\top\right)^{-1}\!\mathbf A \mathbf z_t\right], \tag{44.11}\]

which is a posterior for the long-run effect of a test whose long-run outcome does not exist yet. The same expression handles a metric that a given test could not track. The requirement is that the missingness is unrelated to the effects.

Student-t. True effects in online experiments have more large outliers than a Gaussian allows. Replacing the prior with a multivariate Student-t, \(\boldsymbol\mu_t \sim \mathcal T(\boldsymbol\eta, \boldsymbol\Omega, \gamma)\), shrinks a surprising estimate less. The posterior mean is no longer linear in \(\mathbf z_t\).

Dirichlet process mixture (DPM). The most flexible option drops the parametric family. Tests belong to latent clusters, each with its own Gaussian, and the number of clusters is inferred:

\[ \boldsymbol\mu_t \mid c_t \sim \mathcal N\!\left(\boldsymbol\eta_{c_t}, \boldsymbol\Omega_{c_t}\right), \qquad c_t \mid \boldsymbol\pi \sim \text{Categorical}(\boldsymbol\pi), \qquad \boldsymbol\pi \sim \text{GEM}(\alpha_0), \qquad (\boldsymbol\eta_k, \boldsymbol\Omega_k) \sim G_0 , \tag{44.12}\]

with a Gaussian-inverse-Wishart base measure \(G_0\) and a concentration parameter \(\alpha_0\) that governs how readily new clusters form. A test is now shrunk toward the center of the cluster it most plausibly belongs to, not toward the grand mean. The clusters are also a finding in their own right, because the model sees only \((\mathbf z_t, \boldsymbol\Sigma_t)\) and still groups tests by the profile of their effects.

44.4.5 Measuring surrogacy

The fitted \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) answers a question that OEC committees argue about: how good are the proxies? Following Buyse et al. (2000), the strength of the proxies for the summed OEC is the share of cross-test variance in the OEC that the proxy effects explain,

\[ R^2 \;=\; \frac{\mathbf 1_r^\top \boldsymbol\Omega_{yx}\boldsymbol\Omega_{xx}^{-1}\boldsymbol\Omega_{xy}\mathbf 1_r} {\mathbf 1_r^\top \boldsymbol\Omega_{yy}\mathbf 1_r}. \tag{44.13}\]

A second set of diagnostics says where the precision comes from. Let \(v_{0t} = \mathbf u^\top \boldsymbol\Sigma_t \mathbf u\) be the naive variance of the OEC, with \(\mathbf u = (\mathbf 1_r^\top, \mathbf 0_q^\top)^\top\); let \(v_{zt} = \mathbf u^\top \boldsymbol\Omega_t \mathbf u\) be the posterior variance from Equation 44.10; and let \(v_{yt} = \mathbf 1_r^\top(\boldsymbol\Omega_{yy}^{-1} + \boldsymbol\Sigma_{yyt}^{-1})^{-1}\mathbf 1_r\) be the posterior variance from a meta-analysis that throws the proxies away. Then

\[ \underbrace{\frac{v_{zt}}{v_{0t}}}_{\text{TVR}_t} \;=\; \underbrace{\frac{v_{yt}}{v_{0t}}}_{\text{PVR}_t} \times \underbrace{\frac{v_{zt}}{v_{yt}}}_{\text{SVR}_t}. \tag{44.14}\]

The total variance ratio has a direct cost interpretation: to match the posterior variance with the naive method, the test would need \(1/\text{TVR}_t\) times as many customers. The prior variance ratio is the part due to shrinking the KPIs toward what the archive says is plausible. The surrogacy variance ratio is the further gain from the proxies. Computing the three for each candidate proxy is a principled way to decide which metrics belong in \(\mathbf x_t\). Under the DPM the same quantities are computed with each test’s cluster covariance and averaged.

44.4.6 Estimation

All three models are fitted by collapsed Gibbs sampling. The Gaussian sampler cycles through three blocks, with priors \(\boldsymbol\eta \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\eta_0, \boldsymbol\Phi)\) and \(\boldsymbol\Omega \sim \mathcal W^{-1}(\boldsymbol\Psi, \nu)\):

  1. Draw \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) from \(\mathcal W^{-1}\big(\boldsymbol\Psi + \sum_t (\boldsymbol\mu_t - \boldsymbol\eta)(\boldsymbol\mu_t - \boldsymbol\eta)^\top,\; \nu + T\big)\).
  2. Draw \(\boldsymbol\eta\) with the \(\boldsymbol\mu_t\) integrated out, from \(\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\eta_T, \boldsymbol\Phi_T)\) with \(\boldsymbol\Phi_T = \big[\boldsymbol\Phi^{-1} + \sum_t (\boldsymbol\Omega + \boldsymbol\Sigma_t)^{-1}\big]^{-1}\) and \(\boldsymbol\eta_T = \boldsymbol\Phi_T\big[\boldsymbol\Phi^{-1}\boldsymbol\eta_0 + \sum_t (\boldsymbol\Omega + \boldsymbol\Sigma_t)^{-1}\mathbf z_t\big]\).
  3. Draw each \(\boldsymbol\mu_t\) from Equation 44.10.

The Student-t sampler adds a latent scale per test, \(d_t \sim \chi^2(\gamma)\) with \(\boldsymbol\mu_t \mid d_t \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\eta, (\gamma/d_t)\, \boldsymbol\Omega)\), which restores conjugacy; every \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) above is rescaled by \(\gamma/d_t\), the scales are drawn from a gamma distribution, and \(\gamma\) gets a Metropolis step. The DPM sampler reassigns each test to a cluster with probability proportional to the cluster’s size times the posterior predictive density of \(\boldsymbol\mu_t\) under that cluster (a multivariate Student-t), or to a new cluster with probability proportional to \(\alpha_0\) times the prior predictive density (Neal 2000, algorithm 3), and then runs the Gaussian blocks within each cluster. The concentration parameter is updated by the data-augmentation step of Escobar and West (1995).

The authors recommend weakly informative hyperpriors: \(\boldsymbol\eta_0 = \mathbf 0\) (the average change does nothing), a diffuse \(\boldsymbol\Phi\), a small \(\nu\), a prior on \(\gamma\) that covers roughly 5 to 10 degrees of freedom, and \(\alpha_0\) between 0.5 and 2. Cost scales linearly in the number of tests for the Gaussian and Student-t models, as \(T \log T\) for the DPM, and as \(p^3\) in the number of metrics, so the practical range is around ten metrics or fewer. On 190 tests with five metrics and 30,000 draws, the authors report 1.35 minutes for the Gaussian model with \(\boldsymbol\eta\) fixed at zero, 2.45 for the Gaussian, 4.73 for the Student-t, and 142.53 for the DPM. Tests with several treatment arms are handled by stacking the arms’ effect vectors and using their joint covariance.

44.4.7 What the paper finds

Simulation. The authors fit the DPM to the Zillow archive, draw 100 synthetic archives from its posterior predictive distribution (transformed so that nothing confidential survives), and run six methods on each: the naive estimator (N), a Gaussian model with the prior mean fixed at zero (G-0), the Gaussian (G), the Student-t (T), the DPM, and a metaregression (MR) in which each test’s cluster is known, as it would be if tests were tagged by type. Table 44.1 reproduces their headline table.

Three patterns are visible. Every meta-analytic method beats the naive one on every criterion, and the largest single step is from N to G-0: most of the gain comes from having a prior at all. The naive method overstates the value of what it ships by 0.48, about half its own mean absolute error, while the meta-analytic methods are within 0.02 of zero. And the intervals from the meta-analytic methods are less than a fifth as long yet cover slightly more than 95%, the mild overcoverage being the price of hyperpriors that were deliberately not tuned to the truth. The DPM and MR cut wrong decisions by more than half relative to the naive method (from 19% to 9% and 7%).

The Zillow archive. The application uses 190 tests run during part of 2022 to 2024: email campaigns, site design changes, new features, personalization models. The KPIs are the rescaled dollar impact per customer on two undisclosed lines of business, the OEC is their sum, and three undisclosed short-term metrics serve as proxies. Ground truth is unavailable, so the authors split each test’s customers in half, fit every method on one half, and score its predictions against the naive estimate from the other half, which is noisy but unbiased under minimal assumptions.

On that test the meta-analytic methods predict the held-out estimate better than the naive method in 69% to 73% of tests. The DPM’s log absolute error is lower by 0.29, about 25% less absolute error; the Student-t is close behind at 0.27, and the two Gaussian models are at 0.21 to 0.22. All five methods have prediction-interval coverage between 0.94 and 0.96, and the DPM’s median interval is about a quarter shorter than the naive one (1.55 against 2.06). These gains are smaller than in the simulation because the yardstick is itself a noisy half-sample estimate. The sharpest diagnostic is the rank correlation between a method’s prediction and its own prediction error. For the naive method it is −0.59: the bigger the claimed win, the bigger the subsequent disappointment. For the DPM it is −0.14. A second set of hyperpriors that changes almost every setting leaves the ordering of the methods intact.

Fitted to the full data, the DPM gives the surrogacy measures in Table 44.2.

The table deserves a careful reading, because it qualifies the paper’s own framing. A TVR of 0.15 means the posterior standard deviation of the OEC is about 60% smaller than the naive standard error, the equivalent of a test six to ten times larger. But the decomposition shows that almost all of that comes from the PVR: shrinking the noisy KPI estimates toward the archive’s distribution does the work, and the proxies add a further 7% to 12% reduction in variance on top. The proxies are moderately strong surrogates (\(R^2\) around 0.5) and still contribute little, since the prior has already removed most of the noise they could have removed. In this archive the method earns its keep as a shrinkage estimator first and as a surrogate model second. Where the proxies become indispensable is the early readout of Equation 44.11, when the KPI has not been observed at all.

The DPM finds a posterior mean of 7.2 clusters (95% interval 4 to 12), and the clusters are interpretable after the fact: one is dominated by tests of rental search, another contains only mobile tests. The authors suggest using such clusters to discover the metadata a metaregression should condition on. Posterior predictive checks for dependence between the effects and their sampling variances give a smallest p-value of 0.05 across ten comparisons, little evidence against exchangeability.

44.4.8 Replication

The Zillow data are confidential, and the authors’ replication package (synthetic archives and Python code) sits behind a registration form on the INFORMS site, so it was not used here. What follows is an independent implementation in R, written from the paper’s Section 4 and Appendix B, in replication/oec-meta/ of the book’s repository. It reproduces the estimators and the design of the simulation study, not the paper’s numbers, because the data-generating process is ours.

The Gaussian model is short enough to run inline. The chunk below simulates an archive of 190 tests with one noisy KPI and two precise proxies, learns \((\boldsymbol\eta, \boldsymbol\Omega)\) by the EM algorithm (an empirical-Bayes shortcut that plugs in point estimates where the paper integrates over a posterior), and compares three estimates of each test’s long-run effect: the naive one, the BLUP of Equation 44.10, and the early readout of Equation 44.11 that never sees the KPI.

Code
set.seed(47)

# --- An archive of 190 past A/B tests ----------------------------------------
# Three metrics per test: y = effect on six-month revenue per customer (the KPI),
# x1 = effect on click-through, x2 = effect on form-fill rate (the proxies).
n_tests <- 190; p <- 3
eta   <- c(0.05, 0.10, 0.08)                        # average true effect
sd_mu <- c(0.30, 0.40, 0.35)
R_mu  <- matrix(c(1, .7, .6,  .7, 1, .5,  .6, .5, 1), p, p)
Omega <- diag(sd_mu) %*% R_mu %*% diag(sd_mu)       # cross-test covariance of true effects
mu    <- sweep(matrix(rnorm(n_tests * p), n_tests) %*% chol(Omega), 2, eta, "+")

# Sampling noise: the KPI is rare and slow, so it is far noisier than the proxies.
size  <- rlnorm(n_tests, 0, 0.6)                    # tests differ in sample size
C_err <- matrix(c(1, .3, .3,  .3, 1, .2,  .3, .2, 1), p, p)
Sigma <- lapply(size, function(h) { s <- c(0.50, 0.12, 0.15) / sqrt(h)
                                    diag(s) %*% C_err %*% diag(s) })
z <- t(sapply(seq_len(n_tests), function(t)
  mu[t, ] + drop(rnorm(p) %*% chol(Sigma[[t]]))))

# --- The BLUP: combine the prior N(eta, Omega) with z_t ~ N(mu_t, Sigma_t) -----
# `seen` marks the metrics already observed for this test.
blup <- function(z_t, S_t, eta, Omega, seen = rep(TRUE, length(z_t))) {
  prec <- matrix(0, length(z_t), length(z_t))
  prec[seen, seen] <- solve(S_t[seen, seen])
  V <- solve(solve(Omega) + prec)
  list(mean = drop(V %*% (solve(Omega, eta) + prec %*% replace(z_t, !seen, 0))),
       cov = V)
}

# --- Learn (eta, Omega) from the archive by EM (empirical Bayes) --------------
eta_hat <- colMeans(z); Omega_hat <- cov(z)
for (iter in 1:500) {
  post <- lapply(seq_len(n_tests), function(t)
    blup(z[t, ], Sigma[[t]], eta_hat, Omega_hat))
  m <- t(sapply(post, `[[`, "mean"))
  eta_hat <- colMeans(m)
  Omega_hat <- Reduce(`+`, lapply(seq_len(n_tests), function(t)
    post[[t]]$cov + tcrossprod(m[t, ] - eta_hat))) / n_tests
}

# --- Three estimates of each test's OEC (the true KPI effect) ------------------
full  <- lapply(seq_len(n_tests), function(t)
  blup(z[t, ], Sigma[[t]], eta_hat, Omega_hat))
early <- lapply(seq_len(n_tests), function(t)
  blup(z[t, ], Sigma[[t]], eta_hat, Omega_hat, seen = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)))
est <- data.frame(
  naive = z[, 1], se_naive = sqrt(sapply(Sigma, `[`, 1, 1)),
  meta  = sapply(full,  function(b) b$mean[1]),
  se_meta  = sqrt(sapply(full,  function(b) b$cov[1, 1])),
  early = sapply(early, function(b) b$mean[1]),
  se_early = sqrt(sapply(early, function(b) b$cov[1, 1])))
truth <- mu[, 1]

score <- function(e, se) {
  ship <- e > 0
  c("Correct decision rate"             = mean(ship == (truth > 0)),
    "Overestimation, shipped variants"  = mean((e - truth)[ship]),
    "Mean absolute error"               = mean(abs(e - truth)),
    "Mean 95% interval length"          = mean(2 * 1.96 * se),
    "95% interval coverage"             = mean(abs(e - truth) <= 1.96 * se))
}
oec_demo <- cbind("Naive (KPI only)"              = score(est$naive, est$se_naive),
                  "Meta-analytic (KPI + proxies)" = score(est$meta,  est$se_meta),
                  "Early readout (proxies only)"  = score(est$early, est$se_early))

# --- Surrogacy diagnostics at the median-sized test ----------------------------
S_med <- Sigma[[which.min(abs(size - median(size)))]]
v0 <- S_med[1, 1]
vz <- blup(z[1, ], S_med, eta_hat, Omega_hat)$cov[1, 1]
vy <- 1 / (1 / Omega_hat[1, 1] + 1 / v0)
oec_diag <- c(R2  = drop(Omega_hat[1, 2:3] %*%
                           solve(Omega_hat[2:3, 2:3], Omega_hat[2:3, 1])) / Omega_hat[1, 1],
              TVR = vz / v0, PVR = vy / v0, SVR = vz / vy)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.2, 1))
lim <- range(est$naive)
plot(truth, est$naive, pch = 16, cex = .6, col = "grey55", ylim = lim,
     xlab = "True effect on the KPI", ylab = "Estimate",
     main = "Naive: one test at a time")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
plot(truth, est$meta, pch = 16, cex = .6, col = "steelblue4", ylim = lim,
     xlab = "True effect on the KPI", ylab = "Estimate",
     main = "Meta-analytic posterior mean")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
par(op)

Table 44.3 has the paper’s qualitative results in miniature. The naive estimator overstates the value of the variants it ships by 0.31, against a mean absolute error of 0.48; the meta-analytic estimator’s overstatement is -0.06 and its error is roughly a third as large, with intervals half as long. The early readout is the striking column. It never sees the KPI, and it is about as accurate as the estimator that does, because in this archive a KPI estimate with a standard error near 0.5 adds little to two precise proxies and a prior. The diagnostics say the same thing in the paper’s vocabulary. At the median-sized test the estimated \(R^2\) of the proxies is 0.40 (the true value in the simulation is 0.57, and the gap is a reminder that \(\boldsymbol\Omega\) is itself estimated from noisy tests), the total variance ratio is 0.27, and it factors into a prior variance ratio of 0.35 and a surrogacy variance ratio of 0.77. The plug-in intervals ignore the uncertainty in \((\hat{\boldsymbol\eta}, \hat{\boldsymbol\Omega})\), which is one reason to prefer the fully Bayesian version when the archive is small.

The fully Bayesian samplers are in oec_samplers.R: gibbs_re() fits the Gaussian, Gaussian-0, and Student-t models, gibbs_dpm() fits the DPM and (given known labels) the metaregression variant, and both accept a mask of unobserved metrics.

Code
# Meta-analytic overall evaluation criteria (OEC) for A/B tests.
#
# R implementation of the estimators in
#   Huch, Nail, Melconian, Vongsathorn & Feinberg (2026), "Overall Evaluation
#   Criteria for A/B Tests: A Meta-Analytic Approach", Marketing Science,
#   doi:10.1287/mksc.2025.0164
# written from the paper's Section 4 and Appendix B. The authors' own code is
# Python; this is an independent reimplementation in base R (no packages).
#
# Data layout used throughout
#   z      T x p matrix of estimated treatment effects, one row per A/B test.
#          Columns 1..r are the KPIs (y), columns r+1..p the proxies (x).
#   Sigma  p x p x T array; Sigma[, , t] is the sampling covariance of z[t, ].
#   obs    optional T x p logical matrix; FALSE marks a metric not yet observed
#          for that test (paper eq. 6). Missing entries of z may hold anything.
#
# Every sampler returns posterior draws of mu_t (n_keep x T x p) so that any
# OEC f(mu_y) can be evaluated draw by draw.

# ---- small linear-algebra helpers -------------------------------------------

rmvn <- function(mean, cov) {
  drop(mean + crossprod(chol(cov), rnorm(length(mean))))
}

# Omega ~ inverse-Wishart(Psi, nu)  <=>  Omega^{-1} ~ Wishart(Psi^{-1}, nu)
riwish <- function(nu, Psi) {
  chol2inv(chol(rWishart(1, nu, chol2inv(chol(Psi)))[, , 1]))
}

# A' (A M A')^{-1} A for the selection matrix A that keeps the observed metrics:
# the precision contributed by a partially observed test (paper eq. 6, B.2).
prec_obs <- function(M, o) {
  out <- matrix(0, nrow(M), ncol(M))
  if (any(o)) out[o, o] <- chol2inv(chol(M[o, o, drop = FALSE]))
  out
}

# log density of a multivariate Student-t with location m, scale matrix S, df
ldmvt <- function(x, m, S, df) {
  p <- length(x)
  R <- chol(S)
  q <- sum(backsolve(R, x - m, transpose = TRUE)^2)
  lgamma((df + p) / 2) - lgamma(df / 2) - p / 2 * log(df * pi) -
    sum(log(diag(R))) - (df + p) / 2 * log1p(q / df)
}

# ---- the naive single-test benchmark (paper eq. 1-2) ------------------------

oec_naive <- function(z, Sigma, r) {
  u <- c(rep(1, r), rep(0, ncol(z) - r))
  est <- drop(z %*% u)
  se <- sqrt(apply(Sigma, 3, function(S) drop(t(u) %*% S %*% u)))
  data.frame(est = est, se = se, lo = est - qnorm(.975) * se,
             hi = est + qnorm(.975) * se)
}

# ---- conditional draw of every mu_t given its prior N(eta_t, Omega_t) -------
# eta: T x p matrix of prior means; Omega: list or array of prior covariances
# indexed by `idx` (length T). Implements eq. (5b) / (6).

draw_mu <- function(z, Sigma, obs, eta, Omega_inv, idx, scale = NULL) {
  T <- nrow(z); p <- ncol(z)
  mu <- matrix(0, T, p)
  for (t in seq_len(T)) {
    Oi <- Omega_inv[, , idx[t]]
    if (!is.null(scale)) Oi <- Oi / scale[t]          # prior cov = scale * Omega
    o <- obs[t, ]
    Si <- prec_obs(Sigma[, , t], o)
    V <- chol2inv(chol(Oi + Si))
    zt <- z[t, ]; zt[!o] <- 0
    m <- V %*% (Oi %*% eta[t, ] + Si %*% zt)
    mu[t, ] <- rmvn(drop(m), V)
  }
  mu
}

# collapsed draw of a location eta given z_t ~ N(eta, Omega_t + Sigma_t), t in S
# with prior N(m0, V0)  (paper eq. B.2 and B.5)
draw_eta <- function(z, Sigma, obs, S, Omega, m0, V0_inv, scale = NULL) {
  P <- V0_inv
  b <- V0_inv %*% m0
  for (t in S) {
    o <- obs[t, ]
    Om <- if (is.null(scale)) Omega else Omega * scale[t]
    W <- prec_obs(Om + Sigma[, , t], o)
    zt <- z[t, ]; zt[!o] <- 0
    P <- P + W
    b <- b + W %*% zt
  }
  V <- chol2inv(chol(P))
  rmvn(drop(V %*% b), V)
}

# ---- Gaussian and Student-t random-effects models (Appendix B.1, B.2) -------
#   mu_t ~ N(eta, Omega)                      model = "gaussian"
#   mu_t ~ t(eta, Omega, gamma)               model = "t"
#   fix_eta = TRUE pins eta at eta0: the paper's "Gaussian-0" variant.
# Priors: eta ~ N(eta0, Phi), Omega ~ IW(Psi, nu), log(gamma) ~ N(lg_mean, lg_sd).

gibbs_re <- function(z, Sigma, n_iter = 3000, burn = 1000, model = "gaussian",
                     fix_eta = FALSE, obs = NULL,
                     eta0 = rep(0, ncol(z)), Phi = diag(ncol(z)),
                     Psi = 8 * diag(ncol(z)), nu = 8,
                     lg_mean = 2, lg_sd = 1, lg_step = 0.4) {
  T <- nrow(z); p <- ncol(z)
  if (is.null(obs)) obs <- matrix(TRUE, T, p)
  Phi_inv <- chol2inv(chol(Phi))
  mu <- z; mu[!obs] <- 0
  eta <- if (fix_eta) eta0 else colMeans(mu)
  gam <- exp(lg_mean); d <- rep(gam, T)
  keep <- n_iter - burn
  out <- list(mu = array(0, c(keep, T, p)), eta = matrix(0, keep, p),
              Omega = array(0, c(keep, p, p)), gamma = numeric(keep))
  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    E <- sweep(mu, 2, eta)
    w <- if (model == "t") d / gam else rep(1, T)
    # Omega | mu, eta (, d)                                      eq. (B.1)
    Omega <- riwish(nu + T, Psi + crossprod(E * sqrt(w)))
    Omega_inv <- chol2inv(chol(Omega))
    if (model == "t") {
      q <- rowSums((E %*% Omega_inv) * E)
      # gamma | mu, eta, Omega with d integrated out: random-walk MH on log gamma
      ll <- function(g) sum(lgamma((g + p) / 2) - lgamma(g / 2) -
                              p / 2 * log(g) - (g + p) / 2 * log1p(q / g))
      lg <- log(gam); lg_new <- lg + rnorm(1, 0, lg_step)
      a <- ll(exp(lg_new)) + dnorm(lg_new, lg_mean, lg_sd, log = TRUE) -
        ll(gam) - dnorm(lg, lg_mean, lg_sd, log = TRUE)
      if (log(runif(1)) < a) gam <- exp(lg_new)
      # d_t | gamma, mu_t, eta, Omega
      d <- rgamma(T, (gam + p) / 2, rate = (1 + q / gam) / 2)
    }
    sc <- if (model == "t") gam / d else NULL
    # eta | Omega, z with mu integrated out                       eq. (B.2)
    if (!fix_eta)
      eta <- draw_eta(z, Sigma, obs, seq_len(T), Omega, eta0, Phi_inv, sc)
    # mu_t | eta, Omega, z_t                                      eq. (5)
    mu <- draw_mu(z, Sigma, obs, matrix(eta, T, p, byrow = TRUE),
                  array(Omega_inv, c(p, p, 1)), rep(1, T), sc)
    if (it > burn) {
      k <- it - burn
      out$mu[k, , ] <- mu; out$eta[k, ] <- eta
      out$Omega[k, , ] <- Omega; out$gamma[k] <- gam
    }
  }
  out
}

# ---- Dirichlet process mixture of Gaussians (Appendix B.3) ------------------
#   mu_t | c_t ~ N(eta_{c_t}, Omega_{c_t}),  (eta_k, Omega_k) ~ NIW(eta0, phi, Psi, nu)
# Collapsed sampler (Neal 2000, algorithm 3) for the cluster labels, then the
# paper's blocked updates for Omega_k, eta_k and mu_t.
#
# Hyperpriors: alpha0 ~ Gamma(a_alpha, b_alpha)  (Escobar & West 1995 update),
#   eta0 ~ N(0, I), phi ~ Gamma(1, 1), and Psi ~ Wishart(Psi_V, Psi_df).
# The paper puts an inverse-Wishart hyperprior on Psi, which needs a Metropolis
# step; a Wishart hyperprior with the same prior mean is conditionally conjugate
# and is what is used here. nu is fixed, as in the paper.
#
# fixed_c: supply known group labels to get the paper's "metaregression" (MR)
# variant, in which cluster membership is observed rather than inferred.

gibbs_dpm <- function(z, Sigma, n_iter = 3000, burn = 1000, obs = NULL,
                      fixed_c = NULL, nu = 10, a_alpha = 4, b_alpha = 4,
                      Psi_V = diag(ncol(z)) / 2, Psi_df = 8, K_init = 5,
                      keep_Omega = FALSE) {
  T <- nrow(z); p <- ncol(z)
  if (is.null(obs)) obs <- matrix(TRUE, T, p)
  mu <- z; mu[!obs] <- 0
  cl <- if (!is.null(fixed_c)) as.integer(factor(fixed_c)) else
    as.integer(kmeans(mu, K_init)$cluster)
  eta0 <- rep(0, p); phi <- 1; alpha0 <- a_alpha / b_alpha
  Psi <- Psi_V * Psi_df
  keep <- n_iter - burn
  out <- list(mu = array(0, c(keep, T, p)), cl = matrix(0L, keep, T),
              K = integer(keep), alpha0 = numeric(keep))
  if (keep_Omega) out$Om_t <- array(0, c(keep, T, p, p))

  niw_post <- function(n, s, SS) {            # paper eq. (B.4)
    if (n == 0) return(list(nu = nu, phi = phi, eta = eta0, Psi = Psi))
    mbar <- s / n
    S <- SS - n * tcrossprod(mbar)
    list(nu = nu + n, phi = phi + n, eta = (phi * eta0 + s) / (phi + n),
         Psi = Psi + S + phi * n / (phi + n) * tcrossprod(mbar - eta0))
  }
  lpred <- function(x, n, s, SS) {            # paper eq. (B.3)
    h <- niw_post(n, s, SS)
    df <- h$nu - p + 1
    ldmvt(x, h$eta, (1 + 1 / h$phi) * h$Psi / df, df)
  }

  for (it in seq_len(n_iter)) {
    K <- max(cl)
    n <- tabulate(cl, K)
    s <- rowsum(mu, cl, reorder = TRUE)                       # K x p
    SS <- array(0, c(p, p, K))
    for (k in seq_len(K)) SS[, , k] <- crossprod(mu[cl == k, , drop = FALSE])

    if (is.null(fixed_c)) {
      for (t in seq_len(T)) {
        k0 <- cl[t]; x <- mu[t, ]; xx <- tcrossprod(x)
        n[k0] <- n[k0] - 1; s[k0, ] <- s[k0, ] - x; SS[, , k0] <- SS[, , k0] - xx
        if (n[k0] == 0) {                     # drop the emptied cluster
          n <- n[-k0]; s <- s[-k0, , drop = FALSE]; SS <- SS[, , -k0, drop = FALSE]
          cl[cl > k0] <- cl[cl > k0] - 1L; K <- K - 1L
        }
        lp <- numeric(K + 1)
        for (k in seq_len(K)) lp[k] <- log(n[k]) + lpred(x, n[k], s[k, ], SS[, , k])
        lp[K + 1] <- log(alpha0) + lpred(x, 0, 0, 0)
        k1 <- sample.int(K + 1, 1, prob = exp(lp - max(lp)))
        if (k1 > K) {
          K <- K + 1L; n <- c(n, 0); s <- rbind(s, 0)
          SS <- array(c(SS, rep(0, p * p)), c(p, p, K))
        }
        cl[t] <- k1
        n[k1] <- n[k1] + 1; s[k1, ] <- s[k1, ] + x; SS[, , k1] <- SS[, , k1] + xx
      }
    }
