    # Omega_k | mu, c  then  eta_k | Omega_k, z (mu integrated out)   eq. (B.5)
    Omega <- array(0, c(p, p, K)); Omega_inv <- Omega; eta <- matrix(0, K, p)
    for (k in seq_len(K)) {
      h <- niw_post(n[k], s[k, ], SS[, , k])
      Omega[, , k] <- riwish(h$nu, h$Psi)
      Omega_inv[, , k] <- chol2inv(chol(Omega[, , k]))
      eta[k, ] <- draw_eta(z, Sigma, obs, which(cl == k), Omega[, , k],
                           eta0, phi * Omega_inv[, , k])
    }
    # mu_t | eta_{c_t}, Omega_{c_t}, z_t                              eq. (5)
    mu <- draw_mu(z, Sigma, obs, eta[cl, , drop = FALSE], Omega_inv, cl)

    # hyperparameters
    if (is.null(fixed_c)) {
      kap <- rbeta(1, alpha0 + 1, T)
      odds <- (a_alpha + K - 1) / (T * (b_alpha - log(kap)))
      alpha0 <- rgamma(1, a_alpha + K - (runif(1) > odds / (1 + odds)),
                       rate = b_alpha - log(kap))
    }
    P <- diag(p); b <- rep(0, p); qsum <- 0; Oi_sum <- matrix(0, p, p)
    for (k in seq_len(K)) {
      P <- P + phi * Omega_inv[, , k]
      b <- b + phi * Omega_inv[, , k] %*% eta[k, ]
      Oi_sum <- Oi_sum + Omega_inv[, , k]
    }
    V <- chol2inv(chol(P)); eta0 <- rmvn(drop(V %*% b), V)
    for (k in seq_len(K)) {
      e <- eta[k, ] - eta0
      qsum <- qsum + drop(t(e) %*% Omega_inv[, , k] %*% e)
    }
    phi <- rgamma(1, 1 + K * p / 2, rate = 1 + qsum / 2)
    Psi <- rWishart(1, Psi_df + K * nu,
                    chol2inv(chol(chol2inv(chol(Psi_V)) + Oi_sum)))[, , 1]

    if (it > burn) {
      k <- it - burn
      out$mu[k, , ] <- mu; out$cl[k, ] <- cl; out$K[k] <- K
      out$alpha0[k] <- alpha0
      if (keep_Omega) for (t in seq_len(T)) out$Om_t[k, t, , ] <- Omega[, , cl[t]]
    }
  }
  out
}

# ---- posterior summaries ----------------------------------------------------

# OEC draws for the summed OEC of the paper's Example 2 (or any f of mu_y)
oec_draws <- function(fit, r, f = rowSums) {
  d <- dim(fit$mu)
  matrix(f(matrix(fit$mu[, , seq_len(r), drop = FALSE], d[1] * d[2], r)), d[1], d[2])
}

oec_summary <- function(fit, r, f = rowSums) {
  D <- oec_draws(fit, r, f)
  data.frame(est = colMeans(D), se = apply(D, 2, sd),
             lo = apply(D, 2, quantile, .025), hi = apply(D, 2, quantile, .975))
}

# Surrogacy measures of Section 4.1 for one prior covariance Omega and one
# test's sampling covariance Sigma_t, for the summed OEC over the first r metrics:
#   R2  share of prior OEC variance explained by the proxies          eq. (7)
#   TVR posterior variance / naive variance  (= PVR * SVR)
#   PVR variance ratio from the prior on the KPIs alone (proxies discarded)
#   SVR further ratio from adding the proxies
surrogacy <- function(Omega, Sigma_t, r) {
  p <- nrow(Omega); iy <- seq_len(r); ix <- (r + 1):p
  one <- rep(1, r); u <- c(one, rep(0, p - r))
  R2 <- drop(t(one) %*% Omega[iy, ix] %*% solve(Omega[ix, ix], Omega[ix, iy]) %*% one) /
    drop(t(one) %*% Omega[iy, iy] %*% one)
  v0 <- drop(t(u) %*% Sigma_t %*% u)
  vz <- drop(t(u) %*% solve(solve(Omega) + solve(Sigma_t)) %*% u)
  vy <- drop(t(one) %*% solve(solve(Omega[iy, iy]) + solve(Sigma_t[iy, iy])) %*% one)
  c(R2 = R2, TVR = vz / v0, PVR = vy / v0, SVR = vz / vy)
}

To test them the way the paper tests its own, oec_simulate.R draws archives of 190 tests with two KPIs and three proxies from a six-cluster mixture: half the tests are minor tweaks with true effects near zero, and the rest fall into clusters that move one line of business, the other, both, or do harm. The sampling noise of the KPIs is four to five times that of the proxies, and test precision varies on a heavy-tailed log-normal scale. The six methods and six metrics are the paper’s. The scale of the exercise is not: 48 archives and 2,000 draws per fit (500 discarded), against the paper’s 100 archives and 30,000 draws.

The ordering in Table 44.4 is the paper’s. The naive method makes the right call in 72% of tests and overstates what it ships by 0.39. The three single-distribution models are indistinguishable from one another, raise the correct-decision rate to 76%, cut the mean absolute error by about 60%, halve the interval length, and all but remove the overstatement. The DPM takes a second step of similar practical size: 81% correct decisions, error down by a further 30%, intervals 40% shorter again, overstatement of 0.01, and coverage at the nominal 95% where the single-distribution models overcover. On the log scale the DPM’s typical error is \(e^{-0.95} \approx 0.39\) of the naive error, against \(e^{-0.57} \approx 0.57\) for the Gaussian.

Two of our results differ from the paper’s, and both are informative. Telling the model each test’s true cluster (MR) buys almost nothing beyond the DPM here, whereas in the paper it adds two points of decision accuracy; our clusters are well separated in the precise proxies, so the DPM recovers what matters about them without being told. And the DPM beats the naive estimate in slightly fewer tests (76%) than the Gaussian does (79%) while being far more accurate on average. The paper’s Zillow results show the same reversal (69% for the DPM, 73% for the Gaussian). A mixture prior occasionally assigns a test to the wrong cluster and shrinks it toward the wrong center, so it loses a few more head-to-head comparisons and wins the others by a wider margin. A win rate rewards being slightly better often, and decisions about money depend on the size of the errors, so the mean absolute error and the log error quotient are the better guides.

oec_full_data.R treats one synthetic archive the way the paper treats the real one.

Table 44.5 is the use case of Equation 44.11. For 30 tests whose KPIs are hidden, the DPM’s proxy-only prediction has a mean absolute error of 0.15, less than half the 0.35 of the naive estimate that does see the KPIs, and intervals about half as long. Its intervals cover all 30 true values, so they are conservative here. Once the KPIs arrive the error falls further, to 0.09, and the correct-decision rate rises from 73% to 83%: the early readout is good enough to rank tests and to size effects, and the mature KPI is still worth waiting for when the sign is in doubt. On the same archive the DPM’s surrogacy measures for the OEC are \(R^2 = 0.70\) (95% interval 0.54 to 0.83), TVR \(= 0.27\) (0.20 to 0.35), PVR \(= 0.43\) (0.37 to 0.50), and SVR \(= 0.62\) (0.50 to 0.76). Our synthetic proxies are stronger surrogates than Zillow’s, so more of the variance reduction comes from them than in Table 44.2. The sampler also recovers the latent structure imperfectly, as it should with noisy data: the posterior mean number of clusters is 9.4 (95% interval 5 to 15) against a true 6, and the posterior probability that two tests share a cluster averages 0.73 for pairs that truly do and 0.17 for pairs that do not.

44.4.9 Using the method

For a team that wants to adopt this, the paper implies a sequence.

  1. Build the archive. Store \((\mathbf z_t, \boldsymbol\Sigma_t)\) for every test, with the full covariance matrix, fixed metric definitions, and fixed measurement windows. Exclude tests that fail quality checks such as sample-ratio mismatch.
  2. Define the OEC in business terms. Choose the KPIs and the function \(f\) so that the target is long-run value, and resist redefining it when a proxy is convenient. The proxies enter through the model, not through the definition.
  3. Start with the Gaussian model. It runs in minutes, its posterior mean is a linear rule that can be explained to a product manager, and in both the paper’s results and ours it captures most of the gain over the naive method.
  4. Check exchangeability. Test for dependence between estimated effects and test metadata, including sampling variances. If the DPM finds clusters that line up with something observable, condition on it.
  5. Read the diagnostics before trusting the proxies. A low \(R^2\) or an SVR near one says the proxies add little once the KPI is observed, and that early readouts will be weak.
  6. Refit on a schedule and validate. Refit as tests mature, score early readouts against mature estimates, and track the rank correlation between predictions and errors as a running check on regression to the mean.

Three limits should be kept in view. The framework estimates the long-run effect of the treatment as it was run, a short exposure whose consequences are followed for months; the effect of leaving a feature on permanently is a different estimand and needs a forecasting model. Exchangeability is an assumption about the firm’s process for generating ideas, and it can break when that process changes, for instance when a team shifts from incremental tweaks to redesigns. And the posterior for any one test depends on every other test in the archive, so an archive curated toward successes will produce a prior that is too optimistic.

The method belongs to a family that this book meets in two other places. Predicted incrementality by experimentation (Section 14.4) also treats a library of experiments as training data, but it predicts the effect of campaigns that had no control group at all, from features of the treated group, with a supervised learner and no measurement model. Matrix completion across overlapping experiments (Section 14.5) recovers outcomes for treatment combinations that were never run. The meta-analytic OEC is the member of the family built for the most common situation in a product organization: the test was run, the short-run metrics are in, and the decision cannot wait for the metric that matters.

44.5 Difference-in-Differences

When randomization is impossible—a competitor enters a market, a regulator changes a privacy rule, a firm rolls a price change out to some regions before others—the analyst exploits timing. Difference-in-differences compares the change in outcomes for a treated group, before versus after the intervention, against the contemporaneous change for an untreated control group. Differencing over time removes any fixed differences between the groups; differencing across groups removes any common time trend. What remains, under one key assumption, is the treatment effect. Figure 44.7 traces the two subtractions.

Formally, with two periods (pre, post) and two groups (treated \(T\), control \(C\)), the DiD estimator is the difference of differences in group means,

\[ \hat\tau_{\text{DiD}} = \big(\bar Y_{T,\text{post}} - \bar Y_{T,\text{pre}}\big) - \big(\bar Y_{C,\text{post}} - \bar Y_{C,\text{pre}}\big). \tag{44.15}\]

In panel-regression form, with unit fixed effects \(\alpha_i\), time fixed effects \(\gamma_t\), and a treatment indicator \(D_{it}\) equal to one for treated units in post-treatment periods,

\[ Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \tau\,D_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}, \tag{44.16}\]

and \(\hat\tau\) is the DiD (two-way fixed-effects) estimator of the ATT.

Identifying assumption: parallel trends. DiD is unbiased for the ATT if, absent treatment, the treated and control groups would have followed the same trajectory:

\[ \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}(0) - Y_{i,\text{pre}}(0) \mid T] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,\text{post}}(0) - Y_{i,\text{pre}}(0) \mid C]. \tag{44.17}\]

The groups may differ in levels—that is differenced away—but their untreated trends must coincide. This assumption is fundamentally untestable, because the treated group’s untreated post-period trend is the missing counterfactual. What is testable is its observable implication: if trends are parallel after treatment, they were typically parallel before. A pre-trends (event-study) check estimates leads and lags of the treatment and asks whether the pre-treatment leads are jointly zero.

What breaks identification. Parallel trends fails whenever something other than the treatment moves the groups differently over the window—a localized demand shock, mean reversion when treatment is assigned to units with unusually low recent outcomes (Ashenfelter’s dip), or anticipation effects. A subtler hazard has emerged in staggered adoption, where units are treated at different times: the standard two-way fixed-effects estimator in Equation 44.16 implicitly uses already-treated units as controls for later-treated ones, and when effects vary over time this “forbidden comparison” can produce a weighted average with negative weights and a biased—even wrong-signed—estimate. Modern heterogeneity-robust estimators address this, and a careful analyst reports both the two-way fixed-effects number and a robust alternative.

Code
set.seed(47)

# Panel: 60 markets x 12 months. Treatment (a price cut) hits half the markets
# in month 7. The control group is constructed to satisfy parallel trends.
n_markets <- 60; n_months <- 12; treat_month <- 7; true_att <- 1.5
markets <- 1:n_markets
treated <- markets %in% sample(markets, n_markets / 2)

panel <- expand.grid(market = markets, month = 1:n_months)
panel$treated <- treated[panel$market]
market_fe <- rnorm(n_markets, 10, 2)[panel$market]   # level differences (ok)
time_fe   <- 0.20 * panel$month                       # common trend (ok)
post      <- panel$month >= treat_month
panel$D   <- as.integer(panel$treated & post)
panel$sales <- market_fe + time_fe + true_att * panel$D +
               rnorm(nrow(panel), 0, 0.8)

# DiD via two-way fixed effects (unit + time dummies).
fit <- lm(sales ~ factor(market) + factor(month) + D, data = panel)
att_hat <- coef(fit)["D"]
ci <- confint(fit)["D", ]
cat(sprintf("True ATT:        %.3f\n", true_att))
#> True ATT:        1.500
cat(sprintf("DiD estimate:    %.3f  [%.3f, %.3f]\n", att_hat, ci[1], ci[2]))
#> DiD estimate:    1.662  [1.437, 1.886]

DiD is the workhorse of advertising-spillover and pricing studies in marketing, precisely because firms so often roll changes out geographically and at staggered times—exactly the structure DiD exploits, and exactly the structure that demands the heterogeneity-robust care just described.

A platform feature rolled out product by product shows what that care looks like when the platform, not the researcher, chooses the timing. Wang et al. (2026) estimate how Amazon’s AI-generated review summaries affect review volume (Section 13.5.1), and their online appendix covers four checks that any staggered design of this kind should report. (1) Robust estimator next to TWFE. The two-way estimate on log(reviews + 1) is 0.071 without controls and 0.060 with them. The Callaway–Sant’Anna estimate (Callaway and Sant’Anna 2021) is 0.039 and 0.052. Both robust estimates are smaller, which is the kind of gap the forbidden-comparison critique (Goodman-Bacon 2021) says can open, and both remain clearly positive. (2) Model the timing. A Cox hazard model of when each product received its summary includes the outcome’s five weekly lags. None of them predicts adoption, so the platform did not visibly target products whose reviews were already rising. Price and product tenure do predict adoption, which is why they belong among the controls. (3) Use a second control population. The same products on a storefront or retailer without the feature (Amazon UK, Walmart) give a comparison that does not depend on not-yet-treated products. (4) Check the transform. With many zero-review weeks, log(y + 1) estimates depend on the outcome’s units. The authors also report Poisson and untransformed-count estimates (about 0.33 more reviews per product-week), which is the defensible way to state the magnitude.

A government program rolled out place by place gives a third pattern, in which every unit in the sample is eventually treated. Agarwal et al. (2026) study whether India’s rural road program drew households into the stock market (Section 76.6.6), and the working-paper version (Agarwal et al. 2022) keeps only the 4,154 postal codes that received a first road during the sample window. Dropping never-connected places removes the comparison most exposed to selection, since places that never get a road differ from those that do. Identification then rests on timing alone, and that has three consequences worth stating in any paper built this way. (1) The event study loses a degree of freedom. Without a never-treated group, unit and calendar-time fixed effects absorb a linear trend in time since treatment, so two event-time coefficients have to be omitted instead of one. The authors drop the year before completion and the earliest lead. (2) The pre-trend test is weaker than it looks. With two leads normalized to zero, the remaining leads can only reveal departures from a linear pre-trend. The working paper says so, and reports a joint test of the pre-period coefficients (\(p = 0.58\)). (3) Controls run out. A group-time estimator (Callaway and Sant’Anna 2021) must use not-yet-treated units as controls, and the last cohort to be treated has none, so late-period effects are either not identified or rest on few comparison units. The working paper adds a placebo that fits this design well: reassign completion dates at random, 500 times, keeping the set of treated places fixed. The placebo coefficients average zero, which rules out a result produced by the panel’s structure but not one produced by road timing that follows local growth.

A harder case is when consumers choose the treatment. Myeong et al. (2026) estimate what a food-delivery subscription does to orders, restaurant visits and local spending (Section 70.7.2). Each user’s own sign-up date is the event, so the identifying variation comes from self-selection plus timing. Their online appendix contains three checks that carry over to any “adopters versus matched non-adopters” DiD, and one hazard to look for. (1) Look-ahead matching. Compare early adopters with people who adopt later, using only the window before the later group signs up. Both groups chose the product, so selection on the decision to subscribe is held fixed and only its timing differs. Here, the look-ahead comparison (139 users per group) gives +0.089 focal-platform orders a day, −0.034 rival orders and +0.038 restaurant visits. All three match the main estimates in sign. The focal and restaurant effects are close to the main estimates (+0.085 and +0.035), and the rival loss is almost four times larger (main estimate −0.009), on a far smaller sample. (2) A placebo outcome. Choose an outcome that the treatment should not move but that the same confounders would move, such as a general spending surge or a change in how the user uses the app. Non-delivery online spending returns 0.018 (SE 0.013). (3) Separate uptake from use. Dropping subscribers who never ordered, and separately dropping the heaviest post-subscription users, shows whether the effect is driven by mechanical usage among the most engaged. Note that the first of these moves the estimate toward treatment-on-the-treated, whatever the table calls it. The hazard is bad controls. The models condition on day-level activity in other spending categories (beauty, culture, transport, cafés and so on). If those are same-period spending, as their names suggest (the main text was not available to check), they are themselves candidate outcomes, and the paper’s own thesis is that the subscription moves non-food local spending. Conditioning on a post-treatment outcome blocks part of the effect. The no-controls specification is the diagnostic. The platform estimates barely move (0.704 against 0.706 for log amount), but restaurant visits rise from 0.035 to 0.050, which is the direction that over-control would predict. When the controls are plausibly affected by treatment, report the specification without them as the primary estimate, or measure the controls before treatment. A last habit is to check the stars against the standard errors before quoting an appendix table. Two cells in this one carry three stars on t-ratios below 1 (−0.012 with SE 0.018 and −0.001 with SE 0.003). These are probably typesetting slips, but a reader cannot know which number is correct.

In a fifth pattern the event is chosen by a third party. Poelhekke, Vlahu, and Volosovych (2026) ask what a majority acquisition does to the target firm’s bank relationships (Section 10.8), where the acquirer picks the target and the target’s later bank choices are the outcome. The design details below come from the main text of the September 2025 working-paper revision (Poelhekke, Vlahu, and Volosovych 2025); its tables and online appendix were not read. Four choices are worth copying, and one limit should be stated plainly. (1) Difference the outcome when it is a persistent count. The number of banks a firm uses barely moves from year to year, so a levels regression with firm fixed effects has strongly serially correlated errors. The authors regress the change from the year before the deal to the year after on an acquisition dummy, which removes the firm effect and also lets the change be split into banks added and banks dropped. A net change near zero can hide replacement, and the split shows it. (2) Match by coarsening, with the lagged outcome matched exactly. Coarsened exact matching (Iacus, King, and Porro 2012) puts treated and control firms in the same cell of year × industry × country and the same bins of employment, revenue, assets, and growth, and requires the same number of banks before the deal. No propensity model has to be specified, and balance on the binned variables holds by construction. Three matched samples of increasing strictness are reported, and the headline estimate (+0.056 relationships in the full sample) is only slightly smaller in each. (3) Show where the staggered variation comes from. A Goodman-Bacon decomposition (Goodman-Bacon 2021) attributes 92% of the identifying variation to comparisons of treated with never-treated firms, so the forbidden comparisons carry little weight, and the interaction-weighted estimator (Sun and Abraham 2021) and a same-year-treatment subsample give the same answer. (4) Report the matched result when it disagrees. For acquirers from another region, the full sample shows more banks added (+0.064) and no change in banks dropped. In the matched sample the addition is no longer significant and dropped relationships become less likely (−0.029). The authors print both and change the interpretation from expansion to retention. The limit is that matching and differencing remove fixed differences and observed pre-deal characteristics, not selection on what the acquirer expects to happen next. The paper states its identifying assumption directly, that acquirers do not choose targets on the trend in the target’s bank relationships, and concedes that acquirer motives are unobserved. The authors also decline to estimate what the new bank ties do to target performance, because that would require a second source of exogenous variation for bank choice. Stopping at the estimand the design can support is a choice a reader should credit.

44.6 Instrumental Variables

Sometimes treatment is endogenous and no untreated group plausibly satisfies parallel trends, yet there exists a third variable that shifts the treatment for reasons unrelated to the outcome. Instrumental variables exploit that variable to isolate the slice of treatment variation that is “as good as randomly assigned.” The motivating problem in marketing is the price endogeneity that defeats naive demand estimation: observed prices and quantities are jointly determined by demand and supply, so a regression of quantity on price recovers neither the demand curve nor a causal price elasticity. An instrument that shifts supply (and hence price) without shifting demand traces out the demand curve.

Let the structural (“second-stage”) equation of interest be

\[ Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{\gamma} + u_i, \tag{44.18}\]

where \(D_i\) (e.g., price) is correlated with the error \(u_i\) (\(\mathbb{E}[D_i u_i] \neq 0\)), so OLS is biased. An instrument \(Z_i\) identifies \(\beta_1\) if it satisfies three conditions:

  1. Relevance: \(Z_i\) shifts the treatment, \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z_i, D_i) \neq 0\). This is testable—it is the first-stage regression.
  2. Exclusion: \(Z_i\) affects \(Y_i\) only through \(D_i\), not directly, \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z_i, u_i) = 0\). This is untestable and must be argued from institutional knowledge.
  3. Exogeneity (independence): \(Z_i\) is as good as randomly assigned with respect to the unobservables driving \(Y_i\).

Figure 44.8 depicts the structure in the demand-estimation setting that motivates it.

The estimator is two-stage least squares (2SLS): regress \(D_i\) on \(Z_i\) and covariates to obtain fitted \(\hat D_i\) (the exogenous part of treatment variation), then regress \(Y_i\) on \(\hat D_i\). With a single instrument and no covariates this reduces to the Wald ratio,

\[ \hat\beta_1^{\text{IV}} = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i, Z_i)}{\operatorname{Cov}(D_i, Z_i)} = \frac{\widehat{\text{reduced form}}}{\widehat{\text{first stage}}}. \tag{44.19}\]

What IV identifies. With heterogeneous effects and a binary instrument, 2SLS does not estimate the ATE but the local average treatment effect (LATE): the average effect among compliers—units whose treatment status responds to the instrument—under a monotonicity condition (the instrument moves no unit in the opposite direction). The effect on always-takers and never-takers is not identified. This is a feature to interpret, not a bug to hide: the LATE answers “what is the effect for the units a policy operating through this instrument would actually move?”

What breaks identification. Two failures dominate. A weak instrument (low first-stage correlation) inflates variance and, worse, biases 2SLS toward the OLS estimate it was meant to fix; the conventional diagnostic is a first-stage \(F\)-statistic well above the rule-of-thumb of 10, though that threshold is now known to be optimistic. An exclusion-restriction violation—the instrument affecting the outcome through any channel other than the treatment—biases the estimate by an amount that cannot be detected from the data and must be defended by argument. In demand estimation the classic instruments are cost shifters and, following the differentiated-products tradition, functions of rival products’ characteristics that shift a product’s markup without entering its demand directly (Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes 1995). The credibility of any IV study lives or dies on the narrative for the exclusion restriction.

Code
set.seed(47)

# Demand estimation with price endogeneity. A demand shock 'xi' raises BOTH
# quantity and (through the firm's pricing) price -> OLS elasticity is biased
# toward zero. A cost shifter 'Z' instruments for price.
n <- 5000
xi   <- rnorm(n)                              # unobserved demand shock
Z    <- rnorm(n)                              # cost shifter (instrument)
price <- 2.0 - 0.8 * Z + 1.0 * xi + rnorm(n) # price rises with demand shock
true_elasticity <- -1.2
logq <- 5 + true_elasticity * price + 1.5 * xi + rnorm(n)  # xi enters demand

ols <- coef(lm(logq ~ price))["price"]

# 2SLS by hand: first stage, then second stage on fitted price.
first  <- lm(price ~ Z)
phat   <- fitted(first)
iv     <- coef(lm(logq ~ phat))["phat"]
F_stat <- summary(first)$fstatistic["value"]

cat(sprintf("True price elasticity:   %.3f\n", true_elasticity))
#> True price elasticity:   -1.200
cat(sprintf("OLS (biased):            %.3f\n", ols))
#> OLS (biased):            -0.628
cat(sprintf("2SLS (IV):               %.3f\n", iv))
#> 2SLS (IV):               -1.195
cat(sprintf("First-stage F:           %.1f\n", F_stat))
#> First-stage F:           1795.5

44.6.1 Invitations, Not Assignments: Intention-to-Treat Under Two-Sided Non-Compliance

Many good instruments do not assign treatment. They invite it. A lottery offers a voucher that some winners decline. An encouragement design sends an email that some recipients ignore, while some non-recipients find the feature anyway. Two kinds of units ignore the instrument. Never-takers stay untreated even when invited, and always-takers take treatment even when not invited. The compliers are the units whose treatment the invitation actually moves. With a binary invitation \(Z_i\) and treatment \(D_i\), three regressions answer three different questions:

  • The reduced form of \(Y\) on \(Z\) is the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect. It is causal under nothing more than random assignment of \(Z\).
  • The first stage of \(D\) on \(Z\) estimates the share of compliers, \(\pi_c\), provided there are no defiers.
  • Their ratio, Equation 44.19, is the LATE on compliers. It additionally needs monotonicity and the exclusion restriction.

Because \(\text{ITT} = \pi_c \cdot \text{LATE}\) and \(0 < \pi_c \le 1\), the ITT has the same sign as the LATE and is no larger in magnitude. That is what makes it the conservative headline when the extra assumptions are in doubt.

A study of startups born in the Great Recession (Bias and Ljungqvist 2026), covered in Section 30.6.5, shows the logic at work. The treatment, being born in the recession, is a founder’s choice. The invitation is receiving one’s first patent grant during the recession. Two independent sources of randomness make it as good as random: examiners who differ in review speed are assigned quasi-randomly, and nobody filing years earlier could know when the recession would arrive. That is a double randomization, conditioned on technology-field-by-application-year fixed effects. Two refinements carry over to other settings. First, the authors found signs that the realized invitation was not quite random, because weaker applications seemed to get priority during the recession. They therefore instrumented the realized grant date with a predicted grant date, built from the filing date, the docketing lag, and the examiner’s historical speed, and called the result a bias-corrected ITT. Second, they probed the two assumptions usually waved through (Bias and Ljungqvist 2023). For exclusion, they ran a “no first stage, no reduced form” check, due to Angrist, Lavy, and Schlosser. In samples where the invitation does not move founding dates, such as the untreated firms, it should not move outcomes either, and it does not. For monotonicity, they used Dobbie, Goldin, and Yang’s implication that with no defiers the first stage must be non-negative in every subsample. They split startups by inventor-team size, experience, productivity, breakthrough record, and whether the inventors had an attorney, and the first stage stayed positive throughout. Their LATEs come out about three times the ITTs, as the complier share implies.

The simulation below builds that population. Always-takers are weaker “forced” founders and never-takers are stronger ones, so the naive comparison of recession-born and expansion-born firms mixes types. Here it gets even the sign wrong. The ITT is small but correctly signed, and dividing by the first stage recovers the effect on compliers.

Code
set.seed(2007)

# Startups differ in how their founding date responds to a recession-timed
# patent grant Z (the invitation). Type shares loosely follow the working
# paper's compliance decomposition; outcome levels are illustrative only.
n    <- 20000
type <- sample(c("always", "never", "complier"), n, replace = TRUE,
               prob = c(0.20, 0.54, 0.26))
Z    <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3)                           # examiner speed x cycle
D    <- as.integer(type == "always" | (type == "complier" & Z == 1))

# Baseline 7-year survival differs by type (selection), and so does the
# recession effect (heterogeneity). Always-takers are weaker founders.
base   <- c(always = 0.35, never = 0.60, complier = 0.50)[type]
effect <- c(always = 0.05, never = 0.00, complier = 0.30)[type]
Y      <- rbinom(n, 1, pmin(base + effect * D, 1))

ols   <- coef(lm(Y ~ D))["D"]
itt   <- coef(lm(Y ~ Z))["Z"]                       # reduced form
first <- coef(lm(D ~ Z))["Z"]                       # complier share
late  <- itt / first                                # Wald ratio

cat(sprintf("Naive OLS (born in recession vs not): %6.3f\n", ols))
#> Naive OLS (born in recession vs not): -0.068
cat(sprintf("ITT (invited vs not):                 %6.3f\n", itt))
#> ITT (invited vs not):                  0.074
cat(sprintf("First stage (complier share):         %6.3f\n", first))
#> First stage (complier share):          0.257
cat(sprintf("LATE = ITT / first stage:             %6.3f\n", late))
#> LATE = ITT / first stage:              0.287
cat(sprintf("True effect on compliers:             %6.3f\n", 0.30))
#> True effect on compliers:              0.300

The LATE describes only the compliers. In the startup study, these are ventures whose founding date moved with their grant, and the estimate says nothing about the forced entrepreneurs who would have started in the recession regardless.

The treatment can also be a past choice. Gabel et al. (2026) use randomly assigned coupons as the invitation and today’s purchase of the couponed brand as the treatment. The outcome is whether the household buys that brand again on its next category purchase. The LATE is then the causal effect of one purchase on the next (structural state dependence) for households that the coupon moved. That is the parameter that brand-choice models have estimated from observational panels for decades. The exclusion restriction says the coupon affects next purchase only through today’s purchase. It would fail if the coupon itself made the brand more memorable. Section 38.6.2 shows how to compare this LATE with a structural model’s prediction.

An invitation can also expire. In corporate technology pilots the control group is usually given access once the pilot ends, so the first stage shrinks over calendar time and eventually vanishes. Cui et al. (2026) face this in three experiments that randomized access to an AI coding assistant (Section 69.11.6). In a panel with unit and period fixed effects, initial assignment \(Z_i\) predicts adoption strongly while only the treated group has access and weakly afterwards. Each additional post-pilot period then adds noise to a pooled 2SLS estimate without adding identifying variation, and the analyst is tempted to choose the cutoff date after seeing the results. The authors instead weight each period by its difference in adoption between treatment and control (Cui et al. 2025). Periods with a large gap count heavily, and periods in which the control group has caught up count for almost nothing, with no cutoff to choose. The cost is in the estimand. If the effect of the tool is constant over time, the weights only improve precision. If it changes, for instance because the tool improves, the estimate is an average tilted toward the high-gap periods, and that has to be said when reporting it. The same paper reports the non-experimental difference-in-differences estimate next to the instrumented one for each firm. The two differ by a factor of about three, in opposite directions across firms.

44.6.2 Peer Shocks as Instruments: Do Foundations Fill Funding Gaps?

Some instruments come from the other agents in a network. A study of large U.S. private foundations (Lu and Malliaris 2026a) asks whether a foundation gives a nonprofit more when the nonprofit needs it more. A development officer asks the same thing when one major funder pulls back. Need is not observed. The natural proxy is what the recipient’s other funders do: when they cut, the next dollar is worth more to the recipient. But that proxy is endogenous in the same way price is in demand estimation. A recipient that has a good year, with a new program or a strong campaign, draws more money from every funder at once. So foundation \(i\)’s grant and its peers’ grants move together for reasons that have nothing to do with \(i\) responding to need. In the authors’ sample, the OLS slope of the change in \(i\)’s grant on the change in peer grants is positive.

The instrument is the peers’ investment returns. A foundation’s giving tracks its endowment. So when the other foundations funding recipient \(j\) earn poor portfolio returns, they cut their grants to \(j\) for reasons unrelated to \(j\)’s programs. For foundation \(i\), recipient \(j\) and year \(t\), the outcome is \(\Delta\log \text{Grant}_{i,j,t+1}\). The endogenous regressor is \(\Delta\log \text{PeerGrant}_{i,j,t+1}\), the change in what all other foundations give \(j\). The instrument is \(\log(1+R_{-i,j,t})\), the return of those other foundations, weighted by their grants to \(j\) over the previous three years. The regression controls for \(i\)’s own return, its lagged assets, the current grant and the current level of peer grants. The own-return control carries the exclusion argument. Foundations hold similar portfolios, so a bad market year lowers everyone’s returns. Without the control, the instrument would also pick up \(i\)’s own budget shock.

The published estimates are below. They come from the 143,282 foundation-recipient-years in the regression sample. They are drawn from 511 foundations whose grants are recorded in the Candid database from 2003 to 2019, linked to their IRS Form 990-PF filings.

The sign flips. When peers’ returns cause a 10% drop in their funding of a recipient, the foundation raises its own grant by about 2.2%. Foundations fill part of the gap. The positive OLS slope is what a common demand shock predicts. The 2SLS estimate is the Wald ratio from Equation 44.19: −0.222 / 0.996 ≈ −0.22.

The first-stage \(F\) of 12.4 clears the old rule of thumb of 10, but not by much, and that rule is optimistic. David S. Lee et al. (2022) show that the usual ±1.96 cutoff gives a true 5% test only when \(F\) exceeds 104.7. The authors therefore report the VtF interval of David S. Lee et al. (2023), which stays valid at any first-stage strength. It excludes zero for the baseline. In the three reweighted specifications, the first-stage \(F\) falls to between 5.4 and 10.7 and every VtF interval crosses zero. Those robustness columns are uninformative, not confirming. The lesson generalizes: report a weak-IV-robust interval for every specification, because a weaker first stage can hide in a robustness table.

The split-sample 2SLS estimates show where foundations respond:

  • Science recipients: −0.29 (0.08), against −0.10 (0.07) for arts and religion. The difference has \(p = 0.015\).
  • The longest-running third of donor-recipient relationships: −0.45 (0.12), against +0.14 (0.14) for the shortest third (\(p = 0.009\)).
  • Boards with at least one trustee flagged as a related person, the authors’ marker of founder or family involvement: −0.30 (0.08), against −0.03 (0.13) (\(p = 0.081\)). Splits by board size and by the number of highly paid officers show no difference.

The subsample first-stage \(F\)s range from 7.9 to 19.5, so the same caution applies to the splits.

The responsiveness stops at reallocation. At the foundation level, payout one to three years ahead does not move with the grant-weighted peer shock across a foundation’s recipients (0.017, SE 0.023, one year ahead). Payout rates also respond about twice as strongly to negative own returns as to positive ones (3.12 against 1.45 per unit of return, Wald \(p = 0.05\)). University endowments show the same asymmetry (Brown et al. 2014). The authors read this as a preference for preserving capital. Foundations shift a fixed budget toward recipients that need it, but they do not spend more in total when need rises.

For nonprofit marketing, the result says institutional funders are partial substitutes. When some cut back, others partly make up the difference, with an elasticity of about −0.2, and the offset is concentrated in long relationships. That is an empirical case for treating funder retention as relationship marketing, as Chapter 16 does for customers. The replication package ships the Stata code and de-identified grant extracts, with Candid recipient names replaced by random identifiers, so the first stage and the splits can be re-estimated.

44.6.3 The Algorithm’s Own Rule as an Instrument: A Recommender’s Search Radius

Platform data invite a particular endogeneity problem. A recommender shows a product more often because the product is appealing, so a regression of clicks on exposure mixes the effect of being shown with the appeal that got it shown. A study of a mobile location-based recommender in South Korea (Han, Lee, and Kim 2026) finds an instrument in the algorithm’s own design. The service, which the authors call SmartAround, ranks nearby places on proximity, collaborative-filtering popularity and content-based relevance. It launched officially on April 3, 2019, after a beta for early adopters, and it draws candidates from a fixed 400-metre radius around the user. When the service switches on, every restaurant gains exposure, but a restaurant with many rivals inside that radius splits the gain with them.

The instrument is therefore \(\text{Post}_t \times \text{Competitors}_j\), where \(\text{Competitors}_j\) counts other restaurants within 400 m of restaurant \(j\) before the launch. The design resembles a shift-share instrument. The launch is the common shock, and local density sets each restaurant’s share of it. The endogenous regressor is log exposure, the outcome is log clicks, and every specification carries restaurant fixed effects, region-by-time and category-by-time fixed effects, district daily active users and weather. The first stage is negative, as dilution predicts (−0.000394 per rival in log exposure), and strong (Kleibergen–Paap \(F = 316\) on 3.7 million restaurant-days from 16,720 restaurants in ten districts). The 2SLS elasticity of clicks with respect to exposure is 0.078 (SE 0.009).

Because the online appendix runs a check for each IV assumption, the study is a useful model for a paper of one’s own. Table 44.7 lists them.

The outer rings carry the exclusion argument, and they work because the cutoff is known. The radius is centred on the user, not the restaurant. A rival 400–800 m away can therefore still enter the candidate set of a user standing between the two, so the inner rings absorb some of the mechanism along with neighbourhood confounding. The authors treat the resulting 0.062 as a conservative bound. A rival 800 m or more away can never share a candidate set with the focal restaurant, so the 800–1,000 m and 800–1,200 m rings are clean negative controls, and with them the estimate stays at 0.077 to 0.078. Two limits are stated openly. The first stage collapses under district-by-time fixed effects (\(F = 15.5\), estimate insignificant), because those absorb most of the cross-district variation the instrument relies on. The maintained assumption is that no unobserved confounder operates only inside the 400 m radius.

The funnel continues to visit intentions (calls, saves, navigation requests), and here the design asks more of the reader. The visit equation uses the fitted log clicks from the click stage as its regressor, which gives 0.053 (SE 0.002) with \(F = 6{,}587\). The appendix also reports that the instrument does not predict visits in reduced form (3.05e−7, \(p = 0.548\)) and offers this as support for the exclusion restriction. A referee should read it the other way. If the instrument moves exposure, exposure moves clicks and clicks move visits, the reduced form of the instrument on visits must be the product of the three stages. Equation 44.19 says a just-identified IV estimate is the reduced form divided by the first stage, so with this instrument alone a null reduced form implies a null visit effect. A visit-stage \(F\) in the thousands, beside a click-stage \(F\) of 316, suggests the fitted clicks carry variation beyond the instrument. One possibility is that they come from observed rather than instrumented exposure, which would let restaurant appeal back in. The appendix wording leaves this open, and the main text may settle it. Until it does, treat 0.078 as the identified result and 0.053 as less secure.

The simulation below builds the design. Restaurants sit in neighbourhoods of varying density, appeal raises exposure and clicks together, and busier neighbourhoods gain more app users after launch. The instrument alone is biased by that neighbourhood shock. An outer-ring control or neighbourhood fixed effects remove most of the bias. The last lines contrast two ways to estimate the visit stage, and compare the reduced form with what the chain of effects predicts.

Code
set.seed(400)

# Pre-to-post changes for restaurants in 60 neighbourhoods (restaurant fixed
# effects differenced out). Effect sizes are illustrative, not the paper's.
n_hood <- 60
n      <- 20000
hood   <- sample(n_hood, n, replace = TRUE)
dens   <- rgamma(n_hood, shape = 4, rate = 0.4)[hood]     # neighbourhood density
comp   <- rpois(n, dens)                                   # rivals within 400 m
ring   <- rpois(n, 5 * dens)                               # rivals 800-1,200 m
eta    <- 0.03 * (dens - 10) + rnorm(n_hood, 0, 0.1)[hood] # post-launch demand
appeal <- rnorm(n)                                         # unobserved appeal

b_click <- 0.30; b_visit <- 0.20
d_exp   <- 1.5 - 0.10 * comp + 0.5 * appeal + 0.3 * eta + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
d_click <- b_click * d_exp + 0.6 * appeal + 0.5 * eta + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
d_visit <- b_visit * d_click + 0.4 * appeal + 0.2 * eta + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)

# Just-identified 2SLS as the Wald ratio of reduced form to first stage.
wald <- function(y, d, z, w = rep(0, length(z))) {
  fs <- lm(d ~ z + w); rf <- lm(y ~ z + w)
  c(est = unname(coef(rf)["z"] / coef(fs)["z"]),
    F   = unname(summary(fs)$coefficients["z", "t value"]^2),
    rf  = unname(coef(rf)["z"]), fs = unname(coef(fs)["z"]))
}
demean <- function(v) v - ave(v, hood)

ols      <- coef(lm(d_click ~ d_exp))["d_exp"]
iv_raw   <- wald(d_click, d_exp, comp)
iv_ring  <- wald(d_click, d_exp, comp, ring)
iv_fe    <- wald(demean(d_click), demean(d_exp), demean(comp))
vis_iv   <- wald(d_visit, d_click, comp, ring)
plug     <- fitted(lm(d_click ~ d_exp + ring))   # fitted from OBSERVED exposure
vis_plug <- coef(lm(d_visit ~ plug + ring))["plug"]
chain    <- iv_ring["fs"] * b_click * b_visit

cat(sprintf("Exposure -> clicks, true:             %7.3f\n", b_click))
#> Exposure -> clicks, true:               0.300
cat(sprintf("  OLS:                                %7.3f\n", ols))
#>   OLS:                                  0.605
cat(sprintf("  2SLS, instrument alone:             %7.3f  (F = %.0f)\n", iv_raw["est"], iv_raw["F"]))
#>   2SLS, instrument alone:               0.180  (F = 13029)
cat(sprintf("  2SLS + outer-ring control:          %7.3f  (F = %.0f)\n", iv_ring["est"], iv_ring["F"]))
#>   2SLS + outer-ring control:            0.286  (F = 4428)
cat(sprintf("  2SLS + neighbourhood FE:            %7.3f  (F = %.0f)\n", iv_fe["est"], iv_fe["F"]))
#>   2SLS + neighbourhood FE:              0.313  (F = 3879)
cat(sprintf("Clicks -> visits, true:               %7.3f\n", b_visit))
#> Clicks -> visits, true:                 0.200
cat(sprintf("  2SLS on the instrument:             %7.3f\n", vis_iv["est"]))
#>   2SLS on the instrument:               0.159
cat(sprintf("  Plug-in fitted clicks:              %7.3f\n", vis_plug))
#>   Plug-in fitted clicks:                0.615
cat(sprintf("Reduced form, instrument on visits:   %8.4f\n", vis_iv["rf"]))
#> Reduced form, instrument on visits:    -0.0045
cat(sprintf("  Implied by the chain of effects:    %8.4f\n", chain))
#>   Implied by the chain of effects:     -0.0060

The plug-in visit estimate inherits the appeal bias of OLS, however large its \(F\). The reduced form on visits is small but not zero, and close to the product of the stages. Neighbourhood fixed effects work here because rival counts vary a good deal within a neighbourhood. In the paper they vary too little within a district, which is why district-by-time fixed effects drained the first stage.

The template carries over to other platform settings. Find a rule the algorithm follows, such as a radius, a ranking cutoff, a rotation or a capacity, and combine it with the moment the rule took effect. Then use the rule’s known limits to build negative controls, units the algorithm can never reach. For the substantive findings on geographically disadvantaged restaurants, see Section 13.7.2.

44.6.4 Two Instruments, Two Complier Groups: A Prompt and a Stock-Out

Most IV papers defend one instrument. A study of “swap and save” prompts in online grocery shopping (Gonzálvez et al. 2026) uses two for the same treatment, and the pair shows what a second instrument can and cannot add. The substantive question (Section 20.7) is whether a shopper who accepts a prompted swap to a cheaper product keeps buying it. The treatment is the swap, the outcome is buying the alternative on later trips, and the endogeneity is self-selection: shoppers who accept a swap may be the ones who would have drifted to that product anyway. The setting is an Israeli price-comparison platform covering five online supermarkets in 2015, and the category is mineral water.

The first instrument is exposure to the button. The authors compare shoppers who were shown it (4,079, including those who clicked and declined and those who never clicked) with matched shoppers who bought the same product at the same store within 30 days and were not shown it (1,905), in an event-study panel with shopper, retailer, day-of-week and trip fixed effects. The second instrument is a stock-out of the shopper’s regular water, when the same button offers in-stock substitutes regardless of price. Table 44.8 sets the two side by side.

Three features of the design are worth carrying to other settings.

One-sided non-compliance changes the estimand. A shopper cannot swap without the button, so the prompt design has no always-takers. In that case the LATE of Section 44.6 is the effect of treatment on the treated: the compliers are exactly the shoppers who swapped. The IV estimate (21.4 points) and the authors’ matched difference-in-differences on swappers (23.7 points in the abstract) therefore target the same group, and their agreement is a real cross-check on the selection story, not two unrelated numbers that happen to be close. The implied intention-to-treat effect of showing the button, first stage times second stage, is about 8 points. A platform deciding whether to deploy the button to everyone needs that figure, while a brand asking what one trial is worth needs the 21.

An exclusion threat that can be partly tested. A prompt could raise later purchases without a swap, simply by putting the alternative in front of the shopper. The appendix checks this in two ways. Exposed shoppers who did not swap are no more likely than unexposed controls to buy the alternative afterwards (\(-0.010\), not significant). And a heteroskedasticity-based instrument in the style of Lewbel (2012) frees the prompt to enter the outcome equation directly, where its coefficient is \(-0.036\) (SE 0.013). Both point away from an advertising effect. If anything the second suggests that seeing and declining an offer makes a later purchase slightly less likely, which would bias the main estimate down. Neither check covers everything. The first speaks only for never-takers, since a direct effect among the shoppers who did swap cannot be separated from the swap itself, and the second leans on the Lewbel estimator’s own assumptions about the error structure.

Different instruments answer for different shoppers. The stock-out estimate (31.8 points) is half again as large as the prompt estimate. The two confidence intervals overlap, so the gap may be noise. If it is real, it has an interpretation: shoppers who accept a price-motivated swap are selected on price sensitivity, while a stock-out pushes a broader set of shoppers into a trial. Agreement between two instruments is evidence for both, but disagreement is not evidence against either, because each recovers the effect for its own compliers. The stock-out result carries the paper’s mechanism claim for a different reason. It involves no price advantage, so persistence after it cannot be a response to savings. Its exclusion restriction needs its own scrutiny. A stock-out that recurs on later trips would raise purchases of the substitute mechanically, and the appendix asserts that stock-outs are temporary without reporting how often they repeat.

Two measurement choices sit under both designs. Exposure is inferred for shoppers who never clicked: the button is taken as shown if another shopper triggered a swap for that product at that store on that day. The alternative product for anyone who did not swap is imputed as the most common swap target. Misclassified exposure weakens a first stage, and these first stages are strong, but a reader should still ask whether the unexposed controls were unexposed.

The simulation shows the first and third points. Price-sensitive shoppers accept prompted swaps, drift toward cheap products anyway, and are less likely to stay once the price edge is gone. Stock-out swaps are unrelated to price sensitivity.

Code
set.seed(2015)

# Shoppers differ in price sensitivity s. Price-sensitive shoppers are the ones
# who accept a cheaper swap, they drift toward cheap products anyway (baseline),
# and they are less likely to stay with a product once its price edge is gone.
# All magnitudes are illustrative, not the paper's.
n    <- 200000
s    <- runif(n)
base <- 0.05 + 0.10 * s            # later purchase of the alternative, no trial
tau  <- 0.35 - 0.25 * s            # effect of one trial on later purchase

wald <- function(y, d, z) (mean(y[z == 1]) - mean(y[z == 0])) /
                          (mean(d[z == 1]) - mean(d[z == 0]))

# Instrument 1: the prompt. No button, no swap (one-sided non-compliance),
# and only the price-sensitive accept.
z1 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
d1 <- z1 * (s > 0.63)
y1 <- rbinom(n, 1, base + tau * d1)

# Instrument 2: a stock-out. Whether a shopper takes the suggested substitute
# depends on things unrelated to price sensitivity.
z2 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.1)
d2 <- z2 * rbinom(n, 1, 0.535)
y2 <- rbinom(n, 1, base + tau * d2)

naive <- mean(y1[z1 == 1 & d1 == 1]) - mean(y1[z1 == 1 & d1 == 0])

cat(sprintf("Prompt: share of exposed who swap        %6.3f\n", mean(d1[z1 == 1])))
#> Prompt: share of exposed who swap         0.371
cat(sprintf("  Swappers vs. exposed non-swappers      %6.3f\n", naive))
#>   Swappers vs. exposed non-swappers       0.196
cat(sprintf("  Wald estimate, prompt as instrument    %6.3f\n", wald(y1, d1, z1)))
#>   Wald estimate, prompt as instrument     0.151
cat(sprintf("  True effect on those who swapped       %6.3f\n", mean(tau[d1 == 1])))
#>   True effect on those who swapped        0.146
cat(sprintf("Stock-out: share of exposed who swap     %6.3f\n", mean(d2[z2 == 1])))
#> Stock-out: share of exposed who swap      0.534
cat(sprintf("  Wald estimate, stock-out as instrument %6.3f\n", wald(y2, d2, z2)))
#>   Wald estimate, stock-out as instrument  0.223
cat(sprintf("  True effect on those who swapped       %6.3f\n", mean(tau[d2 == 1])))
#>   True effect on those who swapped        0.225
cat(sprintf("Average effect in the population         %6.3f\n", mean(tau)))
#> Average effect in the population          0.225

Comparing swappers with exposed non-swappers overstates the effect, because swappers would have bought the alternative more often in any case. The prompt instrument recovers the effect on the shoppers who swapped, which here is below the population average. The stock-out instrument recovers the population average because its compliers are a random draw. Both are correct, and they differ. The ordering in the simulation matches the paper’s two estimates, but that is one story that fits them, not something the appendix establishes.

44.6.5 A Policy List as an Instrument: Offshoring and Innovation

Governments often liberalize by list: these products may now be imported, these sectors may now take foreign investment. Membership on the list is a tempting instrument, because it shifts what firms do in some categories and not in others. Branstetter et al. (2026) use one to ask whether offshoring production reduces innovation. In November 2001 Taiwan removed 122 electronics products from the list of goods whose production could not be moved to mainland China. The data cover 483 listed Taiwanese electronics firms in 16 product clusters, and Section 28.5.5 describes the measures and the findings. This section looks at the design, using the working-paper version (Branstetter et al. 2021), the only one whose tables were available here.

For firm \(i\), product cluster \(j\) and horizon \(t\) from 2003 to 2011, the two stages are

\[ \Delta \ln \text{Off}_{ijt} = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1\,\text{Affected}_j + \varepsilon_{ijt}, \qquad \Delta \ln \text{Pat}_{ijt} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\widehat{\Delta \ln \text{Off}}_{ijt} + u_{ijt}, \tag{44.20}\]

where \(\Delta\) is the change from 2000 to year \(t\), \(\text{Off}\) is the cumulated export value of the firm’s mainland subsidiaries in the cluster, \(\text{Pat}\) is the firm’s weighted patent count in the cluster, and one is added before taking logs. \(\text{Affected}_j\) equals one if the cluster was liberalized. Each horizon is a separate regression on 3,665 firm-cluster pairs, with standard errors clustered by firm. Long differences are used because the customs data begin in 2000, which leaves one year before the reform.

Ordinary least squares gives a coefficient between +0.005 and +0.008 at the horizons through 2008. Two-stage least squares gives −0.023 to −0.032 at the five horizons where it is significant. The authors’ explanation is a demand shock: a firm whose product is selling well expands production in China and also invests in the technology behind it, which pushes the OLS coefficient up.

With one binary instrument and no covariates, Equation 44.20 is a Wald ratio:

\[ \hat\beta_1 = \frac{\overline{\Delta \ln \text{Pat}}_{\text{affected}} - \overline{\Delta \ln \text{Pat}}_{\text{unaffected}}} {\overline{\Delta \ln \text{Off}}_{\text{affected}} - \overline{\Delta \ln \text{Off}}_{\text{unaffected}}}. \tag{44.21}\]

The design is therefore a comparison of patent growth in liberalized and non-liberalized clusters, scaled by the difference in offshoring growth. Anything else that made patenting grow at different rates in the two groups of clusters is in the numerator. Table 44.9 goes through the checks this implies.

Three lessons apply to any list-based instrument.

First, count the units at which the instrument varies. A list assigns treatment to categories, and there are rarely many of them. Thousands of firm-category observations do not add independent variation in the instrument. With few assigned units, report inference that respects the assignment level, such as a wild cluster bootstrap or a permutation of which categories are treated, next to the conventional errors.

Second, a strong first stage in the full sample says nothing about a subsample. Heterogeneity analysis in IV re-estimates the first stage on each split, and one split can be weak when the pooled sample is not. Report the first-stage \(F\) for every split and treat a weak one as uninformative, whatever its coefficient.

Third, fix the units before looking at outcomes. When categories must be aggregated, aggregate them on pre-period information only. Grouping on post-period outcomes and on the instrument makes the comparison groups a function of the result.

The estimate is a local average effect for firm-cluster pairs whose mainland exports rose because the product was liberalized. The sample keeps 483 of 792 listed electronics firms, those with at least some patenting or mainland exporting, so it describes the larger multinational firms and not the sector as a whole.

44.7 Regression Discontinuity

A regression discontinuity design exploits rules that assign treatment based on whether a continuous running variable crosses a known cutoff. A customer becomes a “gold-tier” member at 1,000 loyalty points; a buyer earns free shipping at a $50 basket; an ad campaign targets ZIP codes above a median-income threshold. Units just below and just above the cutoff are, in every respect other than treatment, nearly identical—their assignment is determined by a sliver of the running variable that is plausibly as good as random. Comparing outcomes just above versus just below the threshold therefore identifies the treatment effect at the cutoff.

Let \(X_i\) be the running variable, \(c\) the cutoff, and treatment \(D_i = \mathbf{1}\{X_i \geq c\}\) in the sharp design. The estimand is the jump in the conditional expectation of the outcome at the cutoff,

\[ \tau_{\text{RD}} = \lim_{x \downarrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c} \mathbb{E}[Y_i \mid X_i = x]. \tag{44.22}\]

In practice \(\tau_{\text{RD}}\) is estimated by fitting flexible regressions—usually local linear regressions within a bandwidth \(h\) around \(c\)—separately on each side and reading off the gap at \(c\). In the fuzzy design, crossing the cutoff changes the probability of treatment rather than treatment itself; the jump in outcomes is then scaled by the jump in treatment probability, making fuzzy RD a local IV with cutoff-crossing as the instrument.

Identifying assumption: continuity. RD identifies the effect at the cutoff if the potential outcomes \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0) \mid X_i = x]\) and \(\mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) \mid X_i = x]\) are continuous in \(x\) at \(c\)—that is, nothing other than treatment jumps at the threshold. Then any discontinuity in the observed outcome must be caused by the treatment.

What breaks identification. The fatal threat is manipulation of the running variable: if units can precisely control which side of the cutoff they land on—a customer nudging a basket to exactly $50, a salesperson booking revenue to clear a quota—then those who sort just above the cutoff differ systematically from those just below, and continuity fails. The standard diagnostic is the McCrary density test: a discontinuity in the density of \(X\) at \(c\) signals sorting. Two further practices guard validity: confirm that pre-determined covariates do not jump at the cutoff (a placebo RD on baseline characteristics), and show the estimate is robust to bandwidth choice, since RD trades bias (wide bandwidth, more extrapolation) against variance (narrow bandwidth, fewer observations). The estimand is also intrinsically local: RD recovers the effect only at \(c\) and need not generalize to units far from the threshold.

Code
set.seed(47)

# Running variable: loyalty points. Treatment at >= 1000. Smooth baseline
# relationship between points and spending PLUS a true jump of 8 at the cutoff.
n <- 4000; cutoff <- 1000; true_jump <- 8
points  <- runif(n, 600, 1400)
D       <- as.integer(points >= cutoff)
spend   <- 20 + 0.03 * (points - cutoff) + true_jump * D + rnorm(n, 0, 4)

# Local linear RD within a bandwidth, separate slopes each side.
h <- 150
inb <- abs(points - cutoff) <= h
rd_fit <- lm(spend ~ D + I(points - cutoff) + D:I(points - cutoff),
             data = data.frame(spend, D, points), subset = inb)
jump_hat <- coef(rd_fit)["D"]
cat(sprintf("True jump at cutoff: %.3f\n", true_jump))
#> True jump at cutoff: 8.000
cat(sprintf("RD estimate:         %.3f\n", jump_hat))
#> RD estimate:         8.899

s <- sample(n, 400)
plot(points[s], spend[s], pch = 16, col = "grey70", cex = 0.6,
     xlab = "Loyalty points (running variable)", ylab = "Spending")
abline(v = cutoff, lty = 3)
gl <- seq(cutoff - h, cutoff, length.out = 50)
gr <- seq(cutoff, cutoff + h, length.out = 50)
predl <- predict(rd_fit, data.frame(D = 0, points = gl))
predr <- predict(rd_fit, data.frame(D = 1, points = gr))
lines(gl, predl, lwd = 3); lines(gr, predr, lwd = 3)

The simulation is sharp; eligibility rules in the field rarely are. Hotchkiss, Iverson, and Zheng (2026) supply a fuzzy design with every diagnostic on display. Subchapter V, a streamlined bankruptcy procedure for small businesses, is open only to debtors whose noncontingent liabilities do not exceed $7.5 million. But eligible firms may still choose traditional Chapter 11, and a dozen cases above the line were admitted after courts classified some of their debts as contingent, so crossing the cutoff shifts the probability of treatment. Firms just below it are 41.9 percentage points more likely to use the procedure (first-stage \(F = 71.23\)). Scaling the jump in plan confirmations by that first stage gives a 32.0-point increase within $4 to $11 million of liabilities and 49.5 points within $6 to $9 million, where identification is most credible but the first-stage \(F\) falls to 19.71.

Three features are worth copying. The running variable was not in the administrative data: reported total liabilities include contingent and unliquidated claims that do not count toward eligibility, so the authors hand-collected each debtor’s schedules of claims to measure it. The validity checks are the full set described above: a McCrary test (\(p = 0.25\)), six covariates smooth individually and jointly, a donut that drops cases between $7 and $7.5 million, second-order polynomials, and a placebo cutoff at $4 million. And the threat specific to this setting is not manipulation but entry, since a more generous procedure could change which firms file at all; the authors bound that possibility rather than assume it away (Section 30.6.3). The same reform also supports a difference-in-differences comparison with pre-2020 filings. Its 12.5-point intent-to-treat estimate, divided by the 0.42 first stage, implies roughly 30 points, so two designs resting on different assumptions arrive at nearly the same local effect.

44.7.1 Stacked Discontinuities: Unbundling Two Policies at One Cutoff

Regulation rarely changes one thing at a time. A consumer-protection law that standardizes a product usually also rewrites how its price is disclosed, so a single RD at the eligibility cutoff identifies the bundle, not either part. When the components arrive at different dates, the same cutoff can be read in several periods and the parts recovered by differencing. Kulkarni, Truffa, and Iberti (2026b) do this for consumer loans in Chile.

Two laws set up the design. Law 20.448 (2011) created the Universal Credit Contract: for consumer loans below 1,000 UF (Unidad de Fomento, an inflation-indexed unit of account), banks had to show prospective borrowers a standardized contract that limited the fees that could be charged and disclosed costs in a uniform format. Borrowers could still take a different loan. Law 20.555 (2012) then extended the disclosure rules to all loans, while the standardized product stayed below the cutoff only. Reading the 1,000-UF line in each period gives three discontinuities:

Subtracting the pre-period jump from each later one is a difference-in-discontinuities (Grembi, Nannicini, and Troiano 2016). It removes anything else that happens at 1,000 UF, such as banks pricing round amounts differently, as long as that other jump is stable over time. The manipulation threat is unusually weak here. Loans are written in pesos, the cutoff is in UF, and the exchange rate moves daily, so a borrower aiming at a peso amount cannot easily land on a chosen side of the UF line. The authors still show density tests on both scales. Two further tools address the locality of RD: a Cox hazard model estimated around the cutoff, and the conditional-independence approach of Angrist and Rokkanen (2015), which uses covariates to extrapolate the effect away from the cutoff.

The data are loan-level records of the Chilean financial regulator (CMF) for regulated banks from 2009 to 2015. Disclosure reduces delinquency by 13.7 percentage points, a 40% fall, and default by 1.68 points, a 98% fall. Standardization has no effect. Disclosure does not change initial loan terms, so it appears to work by improving borrowers’ understanding of what they owe, not by steering them to cheaper loans. For a marketer this separates two levers that are usually pulled together: making a price legible versus restricting what can be priced (Chapter 20).

The simulation builds the three periods with a true disclosure effect of \(-0.137\), a zero standardization effect, and a small pre-existing jump at the cutoff that a single-period RD would wrongly attribute to policy.

Code
set.seed(2011)

# Loan size in UF around the 1,000-UF cutoff; treatment applies BELOW it.
# Baseline delinquency ~0.34 with a smooth slope, plus a pre-existing jump
# of +0.03 just below 1,000 (e.g., bank practice at round amounts).
n_per  <- 30000; cutoff <- 1000; h <- 80
eff_D  <- -0.137; eff_S <- 0; pre_jump <- 0.03

sim_period <- function(period) {
  x     <- runif(n_per, 700, 1300)
  below <- as.integer(x < cutoff)
  D <- switch(period, pre = 0 * below, y2011 = below, post = rep(1L, n_per))
  S <- switch(period, pre = 0 * below, y2011 = below, post = below)
  p <- 0.34 + 0.0001 * (x - cutoff) + pre_jump * below + eff_D * D + eff_S * S
  data.frame(period, x, below, y = rbinom(n_per, 1, pmin(pmax(p, 0), 1)))
}

rd_jump <- function(d) {                  # local linear, separate slopes
  d <- d[abs(d$x - cutoff) <= h, ]
  coef(lm(y ~ below * I(x - cutoff), data = d))["below"]
}

periods <- c(pre = "pre", y2011 = "y2011", post = "post")
jumps   <- sapply(periods, function(p) unname(rd_jump(sim_period(p))))
bundle <- jumps["y2011"] - jumps["pre"]   # standardization + disclosure
stand  <- jumps["post"]  - jumps["pre"]   # standardization alone
disc   <- bundle - stand                  # disclosure alone

cat(sprintf("Naive 2011 RD (bundle + pre-jump): %6.3f\n", jumps["y2011"]))
#> Naive 2011 RD (bundle + pre-jump): -0.093
cat(sprintf("Bundle, diff-in-disc:              %6.3f  (true %6.3f)\n", bundle, eff_D + eff_S))
#> Bundle, diff-in-disc:              -0.125  (true -0.137)
cat(sprintf("Standardization alone:             %6.3f  (true %6.3f)\n", stand, eff_S))
#> Standardization alone:              0.008  (true  0.000)
cat(sprintf("Disclosure alone:                  %6.3f  (true %6.3f)\n", disc, eff_D))
#> Disclosure alone:                  -0.134  (true -0.137)

The disclosure estimate is a difference of two differences, so it carries the sampling error of four local regressions; with real data the confidence interval should come from a joint bootstrap, not from adding standard errors.

The public replication package (Kulkarni, Truffa, and Iberti 2026c) is a model of documentation even though the microdata are confidential and must be requested from the CMF. Three details are worth copying. The paper’s bandwidths (82 UF for the main 2011 regressions) are fixed as named globals, with a switch to recompute MSE-optimal bandwidths, so a replicator can tell exact replication from a robustness check. The rdrobust version is pinned, because later builds move the optimal bandwidth in the third decimal, which shifts weighted coefficients enough to flip a significance star. And a crosswalk explains that the Chilean variable names for delinquency and default are the reverse of the U.S. labels used in the paper. The spot check it reports, a 2011 coefficient of \(-0.144\) (SE 0.070, \(N = 1{,}117\)) on ever-delinquent for borrowers who saw the contract, is the bundle; it sits close to the disclosure-only estimate, as a null standardization effect implies. The article has a corrigendum (Kulkarni, Truffa, and Iberti 2026a), which should be read with it.

44.7.2 Boundary Discontinuities: When the Running Variable Is a Place

The loyalty-points example has a running variable that each unit carries as a number. A large and growing class of designs replaces it with geography: the treatment changes at an administrative line—a state border, a school-district boundary, a media-market edge, a judicial-circuit line—and units are compared according to which side of the line they fall on. These are boundary (or spatial, or geographic) discontinuity designs, and they follow the same identification logic as Equation 44.22 with the running variable replaced by signed distance to the boundary.

The appeal is that economic geography is continuous and administrative geography is not. Two adjacent counties share a labor market, weather, commuting patterns, input prices, and regional demand shocks. If a policy, a tax, a regulation, or a legal regime switches on at the line between them, the pair supplies a comparison in which nearly everything except the treatment is held fixed by proximity. In practice the estimator is usually not a single local linear fit but a contiguous-pair regression: each treated unit is matched to the unit it physically borders, and pair fixed effects absorb the shared local conditions.

Canayaz and Gustafson (2026) is a clean instance. Federal appellate circuits partition the United States, and their boundaries cut through continuous economic geography. Comparing a county’s small business count to that of the county it borders, when the two sit in different circuits, the authors find that a one-standard-deviation shift toward less probusiness judicial ideology predicts a 1% reduction in firm count—an effect that operates through the exit of young firms rather than through relocation. The substantive reading is developed in Section 30.6.

The setting also illustrates why a static cross-border comparison would not have sufficed. Federal circuits are built from whole states, so every circuit boundary is also a state boundary and carries the entire apparatus of state tax, licensing, and incorporation law with it. What makes the design work is that the treatment moves along a fixed boundary over time: circuit ideology turns over as judges are appointed and replaced for reasons unconnected to any one county’s economy, so a county-pair effect absorbs the permanent differences between the two states and identification comes from within-pair change. The residual threat is not static state policy but state policy that changes in a way correlated with the timing of judicial turnover—a much narrower claim to have to rule out, and the general lesson for any boundary design whose treatment has a time dimension.

What breaks identification here is different from what breaks a score-based RD. Manipulation of the running variable, the fatal threat in Section 44.7, is mostly irrelevant: a firm cannot nudge its county across a circuit line, and the paper’s finding that the effect runs through exit rather than relocation is itself evidence that sorting is not driving it. Three other threats take its place, and they are the ones to interrogate.

  • Coincident boundaries. The identifying assumption is that only the treatment changes at the line. Administrative boundaries are notoriously nested: judicial circuits largely follow state lines, and state lines also carry tax rates, licensing rules, minimum wages, incorporation law, and Medicaid eligibility. A discontinuity estimated at such a line recovers the effect of the bundle, not of the component the researcher has in mind. Boundaries that cut within states, or variation in the treatment’s intensity over time along a fixed boundary, are the standard escapes.
  • Spillovers across the line. RD assumes the untreated side reveals the treated side’s counterfactual. Adjacency makes that assumption harder, not easier: workers commute, customers cross, and firms on the control side may be affected by the treatment through exactly the proximity that makes them a good comparison. A treatment effect that leaks across the boundary biases the estimate toward zero.
  • Boundary endogeneity and sample size. Some boundaries were drawn because of a pre-existing economic difference, which violates continuity at the moment of drawing. And because only units near the line are usable, effective sample size falls sharply with the bandwidth; standard errors must also be clustered in a way that respects spatial correlation, since neighboring units’ disturbances are not independent.

For marketing, the natural applications sit where a firm’s decision environment switches at a line the customer does not perceive: designated market areas for advertising exposure, state-level privacy and advertising-disclosure regimes (Chapter 27), sales-tax nexus rules for e-commerce, and franchise or distribution territories. In each case the design’s credibility rests on the same question—what else changes at that boundary—rather than on any statistical diagnostic.

44.7.3 Algorithmic Discontinuities: When the Running Variable Is a Ranking Score

Loyalty tiers and liability caps are rules someone wrote into a contract. A platform’s ranking code is also a rule, applied millions of times a day, and wherever it sorts items by a continuous score it creates a cutoff at every boundary between two adjacent items. Narayanan and Kalyanam (2015) exploited this in search advertising, where an auction’s ad rank sets each ad’s position (Section 57.7). Moehring (2026) carries the idea into a social-media feed, and the case shows what an algorithm-made discontinuity can and cannot deliver.

The question is how much a post’s position in the feed of Reddit’s politics community raises the comments it receives. The naive comparison is confounded in the usual way: inherently more commentable posts collect more upvotes, upvotes move them up the feed, and they would have drawn more comments wherever they sat. The source of exogeneity is the platform’s own code. Until 2017 Reddit kept an open-source mirror of its code base, so the default “hot” ranking can be read off exactly. Each post receives the score

\[ s_{jt} = \operatorname{sign}(v_{jt})\,\log_{10}\!\big(\max\{|v_{jt}|,\,1\}\big) - \frac{a_{jt}}{45{,}000}, \tag{44.23}\]

where \(v_{jt}\) is the post’s net upvotes and \(a_{jt}\) its age in seconds, and the feed lists posts in descending order of \(s_{jt}\). To hold its score, a post must gain a factor of ten in net votes every 12.5 hours. For two posts competing for positions \(r\) and \(r+1\), the running variable is the score difference \(\Delta s_i = s_i - s_{-i}\). Treatment is being listed above the rival, and it switches on as \(\Delta s_i\) crosses zero. The identifying assumption is the usual continuity: a post’s latent commentability does not jump at \(\Delta s_i = 0\). Several features make that assumption credible. The cutoff is relative, not absolute. Two noisy vote streams and two clocks decide which of a particular pair of posts leads at the moment a snapshot is taken. A post that edges its rival by a few hundredths of a log-vote should be no more interesting than one that trails by the same margin.

Four implementation choices are worth copying.

  • The running variable is rebuilt from outside the platform. Feed positions, vote scores, ages, and publisher domains come from Internet Archive snapshots of the community’s first page (the top 25 posts). Comments come from a public archive of Reddit activity. Because the code mirror was not maintained after early 2017, the analysis stops in 2016; the rule has to be the one actually in force.
  • The score has two dimensions. \(\Delta s_i\) combines a vote difference and an age difference, so the cutoff is a frontier in that plane, as with the boundary designs above (Section 44.7.2). The effect is estimated at the origin, where the two posts are balanced on both votes and age.
  • The first stage falls short of one, and a donut handles it. Reddit adds noise to displayed vote counts to deter manipulation and caches rankings for speed, so a reconstructed score sometimes disagrees with the order on screen. Noise in a running variable misclassifies units precisely at the cutoff. Following Dong and Kolesár (2023), the author drops pairs with \(|\Delta s_i| < 0.05\).
