The mismatch that remains is flat in \(\Delta s_i\), which points to caching rather than vote noise, and the first-stage jump is close to one at most boundaries.
  • Estimation is local, then smoothed. Each of the 24 boundaries gets a quasi-Poisson regression with a linear term in \(\Delta s_i\) on each side and a uniform kernel. The bandwidth is the mean-squared-error-optimal choice (Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik 2014), and standard errors are clustered by snapshot. Because rank-by-rank estimates are noisy, a stacked regression then imposes \(\tau_r = \tau_0 + \tau_1 \log r\).

The validity evidence follows the standard pattern. Placebo RDs on pre-treatment covariates (publisher slant, vote score, post age, hour posted) are nearly all insignificant at the 5% level. Estimates are stable across bandwidths, donut widths, comment windows, and polynomial orders. No density test is reported. Sorting here would mean steering one’s post past a specific rival at the moment of an archive snapshot, which is a different and much less plausible threat than a customer topping up a basket to a free-shipping threshold.

The results show how much the naive comparison overstates position effects. In the author’s April 2026 manuscript, moving from second to first place raises comments in the following hour by 58.1% (a smoothed top-boundary effect of 0.458 log points, standard error 0.058). The effect decays with depth: the estimated slope on \(\log r\) is \(-0.164\). The naive comparison at the top boundary is 0.790, while the rank-specific RD is 0.507. Below the first position the naive and RD estimates are close. The author’s reading is that each hour has a top story that would have led engagement anywhere on the page. The same pattern, a naive estimate inflated mainly at the top, appears in Expedia’s randomized hotel rankings (Ursu 2018). (The 2024 draft on OSF used a log(1 + comments) outcome over 20 minutes and reported a 42.5% top-slot effect. Numbers here follow the later manuscript and should be checked against the published article.)

The RD is not the end of the paper. Its estimates become the exposure parameters of a comment-choice model (Section 38.6.1), which is then used to evaluate rankings Reddit never ran (Section 70.6). The simulation below builds the design in miniature. Latent quality drives both upvotes and comments, the hot score of Equation 44.23 assigns the top slot, and displayed votes carry a little noise.

Code
set.seed(4707)

# --- A feed snapshot, reduced to the contest for the top slot ----------------
# Each period, two posts compete for position 1. Latent "commentability" q
# drives upvotes, so the better post tends to win the slot AND to draw comments
# anyway: the selection problem that makes a naive rank comparison misleading.
n_per <- 20000
q1  <- rnorm(n_per); q2 <- rnorm(n_per)
votes <- function(q) round(10^(2.6 + 0.35 * q + rnorm(length(q), 0, 0.35)))
v1 <- votes(q1); v2 <- votes(q2)
age1 <- runif(n_per, 1, 14) * 3600; age2 <- runif(n_per, 1, 14) * 3600

# Reddit's (pre-2017) "hot" score: log10 votes minus age / 45,000 seconds
hot <- function(v, a) sign(v) * log10(pmax(abs(v), 1)) - a / 45000
D   <- as.integer(hot(v1, age1) > hot(v2, age2))   # post 1 ranked first?

# Comments in the next window: the true effect of the top slot is tau
tau  <- 0.40                                      # log points, about +49%
cred <- plogis(0.8 * q1 + rnorm(n_per))           # publisher credibility, pre-treatment
y1   <- rpois(n_per, exp(1.2 + 0.6 * q1 + tau * D))

# The researcher sees vote counts with display noise, so the running variable
# is measured with error near zero; a 0.05 donut removes the misclassified band.
v1_obs <- round(v1 * exp(rnorm(n_per, 0, 0.03)))
v2_obs <- round(v2 * exp(rnorm(n_per, 0, 0.03)))
ds <- hot(v1_obs, age1) - hot(v2_obs, age2)

# --- (1) Naive: compare outcomes of the top-ranked and second-ranked post ------
naive <- coef(glm(y1 ~ D, family = quasipoisson))["D"]

# --- (2) Local RD: quasi-Poisson, linear in the running variable each side -----
rd <- function(y, h = 0.5, donut = 0.05, cut = 0, fam = quasipoisson()) {
  x  <- ds - cut; dd <- as.integer(x > 0)
  ok <- abs(x) <= h & abs(x) >= donut
  unname(coef(glm(y ~ dd * x, family = fam, subset = ok))["dd"])
}
fs <- rd(D, fam = gaussian())                     # first stage: jump in P(top)

out <- c(true_tau          = tau,
         naive_rank_gap    = unname(naive),
         rd_estimate       = rd(y1),
         rd_no_donut       = rd(y1, donut = 0),
         rd_wide_bw        = rd(y1, h = 1.0),
         rd_narrow_bw      = rd(y1, h = 0.25),
         first_stage       = fs,
         first_stage_no_donut = rd(D, donut = 0, fam = gaussian()),
         balance_cred      = rd(cred, fam = gaussian()),
         balance_latent_q  = rd(q1,   fam = gaussian()),
         placebo_cut_0.6   = rd(y1, h = 0.4, cut = 0.6))
round(out, 3)
#>             true_tau       naive_rank_gap          rd_estimate 
#>                0.400                0.804                0.377 
#>          rd_no_donut           rd_wide_bw         rd_narrow_bw 
#>                0.345                0.376                0.358 
#>          first_stage first_stage_no_donut         balance_cred 
#>                1.000                0.871               -0.002 
#>     balance_latent_q      placebo_cut_0.6 
#>               -0.033                0.002

The naive gap between first- and second-placed posts (0.804) is twice the true effect (0.400), because the same latent quality that wins the slot also draws comments. The local RD gives 0.377, and widening or narrowing the bandwidth moves it little (0.376 and 0.358). Remove the donut and two things happen together. Display noise misclassifies near-ties, the first stage drops from 1.000 to 0.871, and the estimate is pulled toward zero (0.345), which is the attenuation Dong and Kolesár (2023) warn about. The balance rows show what continuity means. Publisher credibility does not jump at the cutoff, and neither does latent quality, which no real study can observe; that is why papers check balance on the covariates they do observe. A placebo cutoff at \(\Delta s = 0.6\), where nothing happens, returns zero.

44.7.4 Rank Cutoffs: Medals on a Leaderboard

A feed creates a cutoff between every pair of adjacent posts. A contest leaderboard has only a few, and the platform announces them in advance. Kaggle, the machine-learning competition site, awards bronze, silver and gold medals by final rank. Liu et al. (2026) use the gold line to ask what a purely symbolic award does to the winner afterwards. Gold medallists enter fewer later contests and contribute more to the community: they post more often, write longer posts, receive more upvotes and share more code. Bronze and silver medals have no detectable effect. The authors call this goal shifting. The award moves effort out of the activity it rewards and into other kinds of platform engagement. Earlier field evidence on symbolic awards concerned the rewarded activity itself; in a natural field experiment, randomly assigned awards raised retention among new Wikipedia editors (Gallus 2017).

The running variable \(r_{ij}\) is contestant \(i\)’s signed rank distance from the gold cutoff in contest \(j\), and treatment is \(\mathbf{1}\{r_{ij} \geq 0\}\). Every specification carries contest fixed effects and fixed effects for the contestant’s Kaggle progression tier. Three features of the setting are worth copying.

  • The platform hides the running variable until it is too late to sort. During a contest, Kaggle scores submissions on a public leaderboard that uses part of the test data. Final ranks come from a private, held-out part. Among the top 10 on the public board, the correlation between public and final rank is 0.004, and among the top 50 it is 0.015. A contestant near the gold line cannot tell which side of it they will finish on. This is the substantive argument against manipulation, and it is stronger than a density test, because it explains why sorting cannot happen.
  • The other two medal lines are built-in placebos. The same contestants, rules and outcome measures apply at the silver and bronze cutoffs. Null effects there mean the gold result is not about winning a medal, or about the attention any medal brings.
  • Money can be separated from the medal. Some top finishers also win cash. Dropping winners who received prize money leaves the estimates almost unchanged (participation −0.042, posting probability 0.170), and so does keeping only contests that offer money or only featured contests.

The appendix is unusually candid about one weakness. The estimates move with the bandwidth, and they move in one direction. As the bandwidth widens from 0.5 to 2.0, the participation effect shrinks from −0.072 to −0.043, while the posting-probability effect grows from 0.069 to 0.165 and the post-length effect from 0.454 to 1.056. The authors attribute this to smoothing bias. A local linear fit is a good approximation only close to the cutoff, and a wider window brings in ranks where the conditional mean bends. Global polynomials show the same instability more sharply: the posting-probability jump is 0.225 with a second-order polynomial and 0.095 with a fifth-order one. Two things survive every variant. Every specification gives the same sign. And the participation effect, between −0.035 and −0.072, is far more stable than the posting effects. The safe reading is the sign and the narrow-bandwidth magnitude. The rest of the robustness table is consistent: rectangular and Epanechnikov kernels, local quadratic fits, added controls for ten pre-award covariates, and logit and Poisson versions all give the same signs. The appendix’s own code measures are weaker than the posting ones. The number of scripts rises (0.028, SE 0.013), but script versions and lines of code do not move significantly.

Two further designs answer different questions from the RD:

  • Local randomization. Treating the five teams on each side of the line as if randomly assigned (Cattaneo, Idrobo, and Titiunik 2024), participation falls from 0.192 to 0.146 (Fisher \(p = 0.019\)) and posting probability rises from 0.448 to 0.617. This view needs no functional form at all, which matters given the drift above.
  • Silver medallists as controls. A difference-in-differences design compares first-time gold medallists with silver medallists who have never won gold, following Foerderer, Lueker, and Heinzl (2021), over 325,717 user-weeks with user, contest and week fixed effects. Participation falls by 0.091 and posting probability rises by 0.055. This is an average over all gold winners, not the effect at the line, which is why the participation drop is twice the RD estimate. The event study shows flat pre-trends, a participation drop that persists, and a posting spike that settles above its earlier level rather than returning to it.

A last check comes from the platform’s history. When Kaggle introduced medals in June 2016, it awarded them retroactively for 156 earlier contests (1,518 gold and 4,505 silver medallists). These medals came as a surprise, and the same gold-versus-silver comparison finds no effect on anything: participation 0.012 (SE 0.009) on 109,950 user-weeks. The authors read this as evidence that the effect needs an anticipated award, and say the result is suggestive only. A reader should weigh it lower still. Many recipients of a medal for a contest years earlier had probably left the platform, so a null could reflect absence rather than indifference.

On mechanism, the published paper draws on self-determination theory and the needs-as-motives hypothesis. A gold medal satisfies the need for competence that drove the competing, and effort moves to contributing. Nine gold medallists, interviewed in August 2025, describe gold as proof of ability and as release from competing. One Grandmaster adds that competition golds carry far more prestige than the golds awarded for code or discussion. The effects differ across winners. Winners with more previous competition medals shift more toward contributing, those with more contribution medals add less, and team winners shift less than solo winners. The working-paper version explained the same pattern with downward social comparison instead. For a marketer, the design raises a question about status programs such as loyalty tiers (Section 5.5). Reaching the top tier may change behaviour outside the rewarded activity, such as reviews, referrals and help to other customers, as much as inside it. A program that measures only spending would miss that shift.

The simulation below builds the design. Leaderboards have three medal lines, only gold changes behaviour, and baseline posting drops off steeply between ranks 15 and 35, so the fit below the gold line bends as the window widens.

Code
set.seed(2016)

# --- Leaderboards with three medal lines -------------------------------------
# 5,000 contests with 100 ranked teams each. Only GOLD (top 10) changes
# behaviour; silver (top 30) and bronze (top 60) are labels with no effect.
# Baseline posting falls off steeply between ranks 15 and 35, so the outcome
# curves away from a straight line as the window widens below the gold line.
n_contest <- 5000; n_team <- 100
rank <- rep(1:n_team, n_contest)                       # 1 = winner
cut  <- c(gold = 10, silver = 30, bronze = 60)         # last place inside each medal
tau_post <- 0.10; tau_comp <- -0.045                   # true effects of gold

gold <- as.integer(rank <= cut[["gold"]])
post <- rbinom(length(rank), 1, 0.15 + 0.35 * plogis((25 - rank) / 5) + tau_post * gold)
comp <- rbinom(length(rank), 1, 0.30 + 0.05 * exp(-rank / 40) + tau_comp * gold)

r_to <- function(k) (cut[[k]] + 0.5 - rank) / 10       # rank distance in 10s, > 0 inside

# Local polynomial RD, triangular kernel, separate fits on each side.
rd <- function(y, k, h, p = 1) {
  x <- r_to(k); w <- pmax(0, 1 - abs(x) / h); d <- as.integer(x > 0)
  unname(coef(lm(y ~ d * poly(x, p, raw = TRUE), weights = w, subset = w > 0))["d"])
}

bw  <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)
tab <- rbind(posting_linear    = sapply(bw, function(h) rd(post, "gold", h)),
             posting_quadratic = sapply(bw, function(h) rd(post, "gold", h, p = 2)),
             contest_linear    = sapply(bw, function(h) rd(comp, "gold", h)))
colnames(tab) <- paste0("h=", bw)
round(tab, 3)
#>                    h=0.5    h=1  h=1.5    h=2    h=3
#> posting_linear     0.090  0.086  0.079  0.069  0.060
#> posting_quadratic  0.110  0.090  0.093  0.093  0.076
#> contest_linear    -0.061 -0.053 -0.054 -0.055 -0.054

# The silver and bronze lines are built-in placebos.
round(c(posting_at_silver = rd(post, "silver", 1), posting_at_bronze = rd(post, "bronze", 1)), 3)
#> posting_at_silver posting_at_bronze 
#>            -0.001             0.000

# Local randomization: the 5 places either side of the gold line, with a
# Fisher p-value from permuting the medal label inside that window.
win  <- abs(r_to("gold")) <= 0.5
dm   <- function(y, d) mean(y[d == 1]) - mean(y[d == 0])
obs  <- dm(comp[win], gold[win])
perm <- replicate(2000, dm(comp[win], sample(gold[win])))
round(c(contest_diff_in_means = obs, fisher_p = mean(abs(perm) >= abs(obs))), 3)
#> contest_diff_in_means              fisher_p 
#>                -0.043                 0.000

The true posting effect is 0.10. The local linear estimate starts near it (0.090 at the narrowest bandwidth) and falls steadily to 0.060 as the window widens, the same kind of one-directional drift as in the appendix. A local quadratic fit stays closer to the truth over the middle bandwidths, at the cost of more noise. The participation outcome has a nearly straight baseline, so its estimate moves little across bandwidths. Note that the gold side of the line holds only ten ranks, so widening the bandwidth adds data almost entirely from the losing side. The silver and bronze lines return zero, as they should. The five-place local-randomization comparison recovers the participation effect without fitting any curve.

(Only the abstract and online appendix of Liu et al. (2026) were accessible when this section was written. The numbers above come from the appendix, and the main-text estimates should be checked against the published article.)

44.8 Synthetic Control

Difference-in-differences needs a control group whose untreated trend matches the treated group’s. When the treated unit is a single large entity—one country where a brand launched, one state that changed a privacy law, one market where a flagship store opened—no single control unit is a credible match. The synthetic control method constructs the counterfactual as a weighted average of untreated “donor” units, choosing the weights so that the synthetic unit reproduces the treated unit’s pre-treatment outcome path (and predictors). The treatment effect is then the gap between the treated unit and its synthetic twin after the intervention.

Let unit \(1\) be treated at time \(T_0\) and units \(2,\dots,J+1\) be the donor pool. Choose nonnegative weights \(\mathbf{w} = (w_2,\dots,w_{J+1})\), with \(\sum_j w_j = 1\), to minimize pre-treatment discrepancy,

\[ \mathbf{w}^{\star} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \sum_{t < T_0}\Big(Y_{1t} - \sum_{j=2}^{J+1} w_j\,Y_{jt}\Big)^2, \quad w_j \geq 0,\ \textstyle\sum_j w_j = 1. \tag{44.24}\]

The estimated effect at each post-period is the gap between the treated unit and the weighted donors,

\[ \hat\tau_{1t} = Y_{1t} - \sum_{j=2}^{J+1} w_j^{\star}\,Y_{jt}, \qquad t \geq T_0. \tag{44.25}\]

Identifying assumptions. SCM identifies the treated unit’s ATT if (i) the weighted donors reproduce the treated unit’s pre-treatment outcomes closely (good pre-fit), (ii) the donors are themselves untreated and free of spillovers from the treatment, and (iii) the relationship that made the synthetic control track the treated unit before treatment continues to hold absent treatment—the synthetic-control analogue of parallel trends, but enforced on the full pre-period path rather than a single trend. The convexity constraints (\(w_j \geq 0\), summing to one) prevent extrapolation outside the donor support and make the weights interpretable.

What breaks identification. Poor pre-treatment fit is disqualifying: if the synthetic unit cannot track the treated unit before the intervention, the post-period gap is not credibly causal. Interpolation bias arises when donors are too dissimilar from the treated unit; overfitting to noise inflates apparent effects when the pre-period is short. Because there is only one treated unit, inference rests not on large-sample theory but on placebo (permutation) tests: reassign the treatment to each donor in turn, compute the placebo gap, and ask whether the true treated unit’s post/pre gap ratio is extreme relative to the placebo distribution.

Code
set.seed(47)

# One treated market + 20 donors over 30 periods; a brand campaign starts at t=21
# and lifts the treated market's sales by a growing amount.
Tn <- 30; T0 <- 20; J <- 20; true_post_effect <- 6
common <- cumsum(rnorm(Tn, 0.2, 0.4))                 # shared latent trend
donors <- sapply(1:J, function(j)
  3 + runif(1, 0.5, 1.5) * common + rnorm(Tn, 0, 0.6))
# Treated market is a convex blend of three donors, pre-treatment.
truew <- numeric(J); truew[c(2, 5, 11)] <- c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)
treated <- as.numeric(donors %*% truew) + rnorm(Tn, 0, 0.4)
treated[(T0 + 1):Tn] <- treated[(T0 + 1):Tn] +
  true_post_effect * seq_len(Tn - T0) / (Tn - T0)

# Solve for nonnegative weights summing to 1 on the PRE period via a simple
# projected optimization (quadratic loss, simplex constraint).
pre <- 1:T0
loss <- function(w) sum((treated[pre] - donors[pre, ] %*% w)^2)
ui <- rbind(diag(J), rep(-1, J)); ci <- c(rep(0, J), -1)  # w>=0, sum(w)<=1
w0 <- rep(0.9 / J, J)   # interior start: sum < 1, so constrOptim's strict-feasibility check passes
opt <- constrOptim(w0, loss, grad = NULL, ui = ui, ci = ci)
w <- opt$par / sum(opt$par)

synth <- as.numeric(donors %*% w)
gap_post <- mean(treated[(T0 + 1):Tn] - synth[(T0 + 1):Tn])
cat(sprintf("Mean post-period effect (truth ~%.2f): %.3f\n",
            true_post_effect / 2, gap_post))
#> Mean post-period effect (truth ~3.00): 3.313

plot(1:Tn, treated, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "Period", ylab = "Sales",
     ylim = range(c(treated, synth)))
lines(1:Tn, synth, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")
abline(v = T0 + 0.5, lty = 3)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2),
       col = c("black", "firebrick"),
       legend = c("treated market", "synthetic control"))

44.9 Mechanism: Causal Mediation and Moderated Mediation

Every design above answers the same question: what did \(D\) do to \(Y\). None of them answers the question a referee asks next, which is through what. Mechanism is not a refinement of the total effect; it is a separate identification problem with its own estimand and its own assumption, and the assumption is not one that randomizing \(D\) can supply. This section states the estimand, states the assumption, and then works through what a credible pathway argument looks like in practice—because the interesting craft question is not how to compute a mediation model but how to defend one.

Controversy: is observational mediation identified at all?

Mediation analysis is among the most-run procedures in consumer research and among the least defensible as usually practised. The critique is old, well known, and routinely ignored, which makes the sequence worth stating plainly.

2010 — the identification objection. Bullock, Green, and Ha (2010) publish Yes, But What’s the Mechanism? (Don’t Expect an Easy Answer). The argument is not that mediation estimates are noisy. It is that randomizing the treatment \(D\) does nothing to randomize the mediator \(M\). Subjects arrive at their mediator values through their own characteristics, so the mediator is observational even inside a perfectly executed experiment, and the sequential-ignorability assumption the estimator requires (Section 44.9.2) is untestable and usually implausible. A bootstrapped indirect effect with a confidence interval excluding zero is not evidence against that objection; it presupposes the objection away.

2017 — the constructive reform position. Pieters (2017) responds not by defending standard practice but by specifying what better practice would be: manipulate the mediator directly where possible, use moderation-of-process designs, report sensitivity analyses that state how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to overturn the conclusion, and communicate the causal claim at the strength the design supports rather than at the strength the software output implies.

What this means at the desk. These two positions are not really opposed. The first says the standard estimator does not identify what its users believe it identifies; the second says there are designs that do better and researchers should use them. Neither supports the ubiquitous practice of running a bootstrap on observational mediator data and reporting the indirect effect as a mechanism.

The reviewer’s question is therefore not “did they use the right macro” but “what would have to be true for this indirect effect to be causal, and did the authors argue for it?” Section 77.8.7 places this among the field’s standing methodological disagreements.

44.9.1 The Estimand: Effects That Route Through a Mediator

Let \(M_i\) be a post-treatment variable on the hypothesized pathway and write the outcome as a function of both the treatment and the mediator, \(Y_i(d, m)\). The mediator itself responds to treatment, \(M_i(d)\), so the observed outcome is \(Y_i(D_i, M_i(D_i))\). Two effects follow. The average causal mediation effect (ACME, or indirect effect) holds treatment fixed and moves the mediator to the value it would have taken under each arm,

\[ \delta_i(d) \;=\; Y_i\!\left(d, M_i(1)\right) - Y_i\!\left(d, M_i(0)\right), \tag{44.26}\]

while the average direct effect holds the mediator fixed and moves the treatment,

\[ \zeta_i(d) \;=\; Y_i\!\left(1, M_i(d)\right) - Y_i\!\left(0, M_i(d)\right). \tag{44.27}\]

The two decompose the total effect exactly, \(\tau_i = \delta_i(d) + \zeta_i(1-d)\) for either \(d\), which is the sense in which mediation “accounts for” a share of the effect.

The critical feature of Equation 44.26 is easy to miss. The quantity \(Y_i(d, M_i(1-d))\) is a cross-world counterfactual: it asks what would have happened had the unit received one treatment while its mediator took the value it would have taken under the other. No experiment, however well run, realizes that state for anybody. This is why mediation is harder than it looks in a path diagram, and why its identifying assumption cannot be reduced to a design feature.

44.9.2 Sequential Ignorability, and Why Randomizing \(D\) Is Not Enough

Identification of Equation 44.26 and Equation 44.27 from observed data rests on sequential ignorability (Imai, Keele, and Yamamoto 2010; Imai, Keele, and Tingley 2010), a pair of conditions given pre-treatment covariates \(X_i\):

\[ \{Y_i(d', m),\, M_i(d)\} \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i \mid X_i = x, \tag{44.28}\]

\[ Y_i(d', m) \perp\!\!\!\perp M_i(d) \mid D_i = d,\, X_i = x . \tag{44.29}\]

Equation 44.28 is the familiar unconfoundedness of the treatment, and a randomized trial delivers it for free. Equation 44.29 is not. It says that conditional on treatment and pre-treatment covariates, the mediator is as good as randomly assigned with respect to the outcome—no unmeasured common cause of \(M\) and \(Y\), and no post-treatment confounder of the mediator–outcome link. Randomizing \(D\) does nothing for it, because the mediator is chosen, produced, or realized after assignment. A field experiment with a beautifully clean total effect can have a completely unidentified mechanism, and this is the single most common overclaim in applied mediation work (Bullock, Green, and Ha 2010).

The classical three-regression procedure (Baron and Kenny 1986)—regress \(M\) on \(D\), regress \(Y\) on \(D\), regress \(Y\) on \(D\) and \(M\), and multiply or difference coefficients—is a statistical decomposition. It acquires causal meaning only under Equation 44.28–Equation 44.29, and the product-of-coefficients form additionally assumes no treatment–mediator interaction. When that interaction exists, \(\delta(1) \neq \delta(0)\) and there is no single “indirect effect” to report. The potential-outcomes formulation makes both the assumption and the interaction explicit, which is the reason to prefer it even when the arithmetic ends up similar.

Moderated mediation adds a variable \(W\) that changes the size of the pathway itself, so the estimand becomes \(\delta(d; w)\) and the object of interest is the contrast \(\delta(d; w_1) - \delta(d; w_0)\) (Preacher, Rucker, and Hayes 2007). Used carelessly this is a fishing device: with two moderators and two mediators there are many contrasts and one of them will be significant. Used well, it is the strongest observational evidence a pathway argument can have, because a moderator that is predicted by the mechanism to shut the pathway off converts a correlational story into a falsifiable one.

44.9.3 How a Pathway Argument Is Actually Built

A paper that claims a mechanism is making three claims, not one, and the credible papers defend each separately rather than letting a single structural equation carry all of them.

  1. The \(D \to M\) link. Treatment moves the mediator. This link inherits whatever design identifies the total effect, so it is usually the easiest to defend.
  2. The \(M \to Y\) link. The mediator moves the outcome. This is where Equation 44.29 bites, and it almost never comes free: the mediator is typically a decision, and decisions respond to the same unobservables that drive the outcome. Confounding by indication—the treatment is given to those who most need it—is the canonical form in operational and clinical settings.
  3. The exclusion of the residual direct path. Whatever is left over is attributed to “everything else,” so the interpretation of \(\delta\) depends on having enumerated the alternatives.

Four devices do the real work of defending these claims, and they are worth naming because they generalize far beyond any one paper.

Manipulate the mediator, not just the treatment. The cleanest fix is a design that randomizes \(M\) directly, or a parallel or crossover encouragement design that varies the mediator independently of treatment (Imai, Tingley, and Yamamoto 2013). This buys identification of a mechanism at the price of a stronger consistency assumption: the manipulated mediator must be the same object as the naturally occurring one.

Find a condition that switches the mechanism off. If the proposed pathway is real, there should exist a subpopulation, period, or regime in which it cannot operate—and the effect should vanish there. A predicted null under a mechanism-off condition is far more informative than another significant coefficient, because rival explanations do not generally predict it. This is moderated mediation used as a falsification test rather than as a search.

Argue the direction of the bias. When Equation 44.29 fails, ask which way. If the plausible confounding pushes against the estimate—if the sickest patients are the most likely to receive the treatment whose protective effect you are estimating—then the observed estimate is a conservative bound, and saying so converts an admitted weakness into an argument.

Report where the result breaks, not that it is robust. A sensitivity analysis for mediation parameterizes the violation of Equation 44.29 by the correlation \(\rho\) between the mediator and outcome errors and reports the \(\rho^\*\) at which the ACME crosses zero (Imai, Keele, and Yamamoto 2010). The number is interpretable: a result that survives only up to \(\rho = 0.05\) is fragile, one that survives to \(\rho = 0.4\) is not, and the comparison to the explanatory power of observed covariates gives the reader a yardstick.

44.9.4 A Worked Reading: Diagnostic Bias as an Upstream Process Defect

Zhang and Jetley (2026) is a compact example of all four devices, and it is worth reading as a design rather than as a healthcare result. Pulse oximetry estimates blood oxygen saturation from light absorption, and it systematically overestimates saturation in patients with darker skin pigmentation—a measurement bias documented clinically by Sjoding et al. (2020). The paper’s move is to treat that bias not as a device-calibration problem but as an upstream process defect whose consequences propagate through the clinical decision it feeds, and to trace the resulting chain with a moderated mediation framework on patient-level ICU data from MIMIC-IV.

The chain runs: race \(\to\) a biased saturation reading under peripheral-oximetry (\(\mathrm{SpO}_2\)) monitoring \(\to\) undertreatment with supplemental oxygen \(\to\) unplanned within-hospitalization ICU readmission \(\to\) downstream capacity consumption. The reported magnitudes are, in the authors’ estimates: under \(\mathrm{SpO}_2\)-only monitoring, Black patients are 5.2 percentage points less likely than White patients to receive supplemental oxygen; oxygen delivery reduces the probability of unplanned ICU readmission by 4.8 percentage points, a 37% relative reduction; and, in a separate operational-load analysis by OLS, ICU bounce-backs are associated with an 86% increase in remaining hospital length of stay.

The design’s load-bearing element is none of those numbers. It is the use of arterial oxygen saturation (\(\mathrm{SaO}_2\)) measurement—the accurate, invasive reading—as a quasi-intervention that switches the mechanism off. If the disparity in oxygen therapy is produced by the device’s measurement error, then supplying the clinician with an accurate reading should eliminate it; if it is produced by something else—clinician bias operating directly on race, differential comorbidity, differential unit assignment—an accurate saturation reading has no particular reason to remove it. The authors report that with \(\mathrm{SaO}_2\) available, the racial disparity in oxygen therapy attenuates to statistically indistinguishable from zero. That is the predicted null under the mechanism-off condition, and it is the sentence the causal claim actually rests on.

Notice what the moderator is doing structurally. \(W = 1\{\mathrm{SaO}_2\text{ available}\}\) is not a garden-variety interaction hunting for heterogeneity. It is a theoretical moderator: the mechanism names it in advance, predicts the sign, and predicts the magnitude (zero). Equation 44.26 evaluated at \(W=1\) versus \(W=0\) is therefore a test rather than a description, and the contrast \(\delta(d; 1) - \delta(d; 0)\) is the paper’s real estimate.

44.9.5 Where the Argument Is Still Vulnerable

Reading a design this way is only useful if it also exposes what would break it. Six issues apply to the ICU case and, with the nouns changed, to most observational mediation work in marketing and operations.

The first link has no manipulable cause. Race is not assignable, so \(\delta\) evaluated on it is a disparity decomposition, not the average causal effect of a treatment. The honest statement is that conditional on observed clinical state, patients differ in the probability of receiving oxygen, and that the gap closes when the measurement improves. The causal weight sits on the \(M \to Y\) link and on the moderator contrast, not on the first arrow. Papers that blur this invite an objection they cannot answer.

The moderator is chosen by the same clinicians whose behavior is the outcome. An arterial blood gas is ordered, not assigned. It is ordered for patients who are sicker, less stable, or already a source of concern, so the \(\mathrm{SaO}_2\) subsample is selected on precisely the dimensions that drive treatment. The attenuation could therefore reflect who gets an arterial reading rather than what the reading tells the clinician. Strengthening this would mean comparing within severity strata with explicit balance diagnostics, instrumenting the ordering decision with something that shifts it for non-clinical reasons (unit protocol differences, lab turnaround, shift staffing, time of day), or exploiting within-patient timing: the same patient’s treatment decisions before and after the first arterial reading, with patient fixed effects absorbing the selection that determined who was drawn at all.

Confounding by indication runs through the second link. Supplemental oxygen is given to patients who look hypoxemic, and looking hypoxemic predicts readmission. That biases the protective estimate toward zero, which is the direction that helps: an estimate that survives a bias pushing against it is a lower bound, and the argument is stronger stated that way than as a robustness claim.

The mediator is a bundle. “Received supplemental oxygen” collapses device, flow rate, timing, and duration into a binary. Under multiple versions of the mediator, the ACME is a composite over whatever mix of versions the population happens to realize, and the consistency half of the potential-outcomes setup is doing quiet work. A dose or timing measure would sharpen the estimand.

The sharpest test is not the binary race indicator. The physics of the bias predicts where it should be worst: at low true saturation, where occult hypoxemia, a normal-looking \(\mathrm{SpO}_2\) over a genuinely low \(\mathrm{SaO}_2\), is concentrated. A design that predicts and finds a steeper disparity in exactly that region, and none where readings are unambiguous, is harder to explain away than an average gap, because rival explanations do not predict the gradient.

A placebo pathway is available and cheap. An outcome that clinical oxygenation should not affect, or a treatment decision that does not read the oximeter, should show no disparity under \(\mathrm{SpO}_2\)-only monitoring. Reporting that null costs one table and forecloses a large class of alternatives.

None of this is a complaint about the paper; it is the standard by which the design should be graded, and the design meets a good part of it. The transferable lesson for marketing research is the structure: when the antecedent of interest is an attribute rather than a lever, move the causal burden downstream to links you can defend, and find the condition under which your mechanism is supposed to disappear.

44.9.6 A Second Reading: Moderated Mediation on Firm Panel Data

The oximetry study runs the machinery on patients. Singh et al. (2026) run it on firms, and the contrast is instructive because the identification problem changes shape when the unit is an organization observed annually rather than a patient observed once. The substantive result—open-source product development raises gross margin about 4–5%—is discussed in Chapter 28. What concerns us here is the second stage of their design, which is a textbook-clean instance of a first-stage moderated mediation and repays reading as a template.

The chain is open-source development intensity (\(OSDI\)) \(\to\) labor productivity \(\to\) gross margin, with the volunteer contribution ratio (\(VCR\), the external share of observed contributions to a firm’s repositories) moderating the first link. Estimation is by generalized structural equation modeling, so every path is fit simultaneously, with 5,000 bootstrap replications for the indirect effects. The paths come back as follows: the interaction \(OSDI \times VCR\) on labor productivity is 0.069 (0.025); labor productivity on gross margin is 0.196 (0.013); and the direct \(OSDI \to\) gross margin path survives at 0.011 (0.003), which is what makes the mediation partial.

Which path the moderator sits on is the theoretical claim. This is the first lesson and the most frequently botched. Their theory says external contributors are what convert a GitHub presence into genuine knowledge integration, so the moderator belongs on the \(D \to M\) path—Model 7 in the taxonomy of Hayes (2017) —and nowhere else. Putting \(VCR\) on the \(M \to Y\) path instead (Model 14) would assert something different and, here, implausible: that the rate at which productivity converts into margin depends on who wrote the code. The numbered Hayes models are not a menu to be searched; each one is a distinct hypothesis, and the paper should say in words which link the moderator is claimed to govern before any model is fit.

Report the index, not the ±1 SD table. Their conditional indirect effects are \(-0.001\) (n.s.) at one SD below the mean \(VCR\), \(0.002\) at the mean, and \(0.005\) (\(p<0.01\)) at one SD above. It is tempting to stop there and say the mechanism “works at high external engagement but not at low.” That inference is invalid on its own terms, because a difference in significance is not a significant difference. The quantity that tests the actual claim is the index of moderated mediation—the slope of the indirect effect with respect to the moderator—which they report as \(\omega = 0.014\) (\(p<0.01\)). Without the index, a ±1 SD table is a display, not a test.

Constituent terms in an interaction model are conditional effects, not main effects. Their base model (no interaction) has \(VCR \to\) labor productivity at 0.103 (\(p<0.05\)); in the full model the same coefficient is \(-0.003\) and insignificant. Nothing disappeared. In the full model that coefficient is the effect of \(VCR\) at \(OSDI = 0\), a firm with no open-source development at all, which is both a different quantity and one estimated off the edge of the data. Papers lose referees on this point, and the fix is to say which quantity is being reported and, where the variables are not centered, to say that too.

A threshold recovered from a continuous interaction is an estimate. Plotting the conditional indirect effect across the full range of \(VCR\) shows it crossing zero at roughly 35% external contribution, which is a genuinely useful number—it separates firms using GitHub as a development tool from firms running a community. The authors label it “a sample-specific point at which the labor-productivity pathway becomes positive and statistically discernible, not as a universal managerial cutoff,” and that sentence is the model to copy. A crossover point is a function of estimated coefficients and carries their sampling error; reporting it as a managerial rule launders an interval into a decision boundary.

Partial mediation is a claim about what you did not model. The surviving direct path is not a residual to be waved at. Singh et al. (2026) enumerate the specific alternatives it might carry—community governance, licensing-driven value capture, signaling to investors—and concede the direct effect may run through them. That is the honest form of the third claim in Section 44.9.3: name the candidates for “everything else,” because the interpretation of \(\delta\) is only as good as that enumeration.

Finally, notice where the identification actually stops. Stage 1 of their design is causally serious: staggered difference-in-differences (Callaway and Sant’Anna 2021), the de Chaisemartin–D’Haultfœuille estimator, generalized synthetic control, an instrument built from industry peer adoption, and Arellano–Bond and Blundell–Bond dynamic panels, all converging on 4–5%. None of that machinery carries over to the mediation stage, which is estimated on adopters with year fixed effects and controls. The \(D \to M\) link inherits some of the design’s credibility; the \(M \to Y\) link—labor productivity to gross margin—is an association between two outcomes a firm produces jointly, and Equation 44.29 is doing uncompensated work there. This is not a criticism peculiar to this paper; it is the normal state of mediation analysis in firm panels, and the reason the chapter insists that randomizing \(D\) does not identify a mechanism. A paper in this shape should say plainly that its identification strength declines from stage to stage rather than presenting all three stages in one confident register.

44.9.7 Sensitivity and the Mechanism-Off Contrast in Practice

The simulation below makes both points concrete. It generates a chain \(D \to M \to Y\) with an unobserved confounder \(U\) of the mediator-outcome link, so Equation 44.29 fails by construction and the naive product-of-coefficients estimate of the ACME is biased. It then does two things a careful paper does: sweeps the assumed confounding strength to find where the conclusion flips, and computes the mechanism-off contrast in a regime where the \(D \to M\) path is shut down by design.

Code
set.seed(47)

n <- 8000

# --- Structural parameters ---------------------------------------------------
a_true <- 0.40   # D -> M
b_true <- 0.50   # M -> Y
c_true <- 0.15   # D -> Y (direct)
gam_M  <- 0.60   # U -> M   (unobserved mediator-outcome confounder)
gam_Y  <- 0.70   # U -> Y

D <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
U <- rnorm(n)                                  # never observed by the analyst
M <- a_true * D + gam_M * U + rnorm(n)
Y <- c_true * D + b_true * M + gam_Y * U + rnorm(n)

# --- Naive mediation: the Baron-Kenny product, ignoring U --------------------
a_hat <- unname(coef(lm(M ~ D))["D"])
b_hat <- unname(coef(lm(Y ~ D + M))["M"])

c(truth = a_true * b_true, naive = round(a_hat * b_hat, 3))
#> truth naive 
#>  0.20  0.34

The naive estimate is inflated because the mediator coefficient absorbs the effect of \(U\) on \(Y\). The analyst cannot see \(U\), but can ask how much mediator-outcome confounding would be needed to overturn the conclusion. Parameterize the violation by the residual correlation \(\rho\) and re-solve for the mediator slope under each assumed value.

Code
m_fit <- lm(M ~ D)
y_fit <- lm(Y ~ D + M)
s_m   <- summary(m_fit)$sigma
s_y   <- summary(y_fit)$sigma

# Under an assumed error correlation rho, the mediator slope loses the part of
# the M-Y association that rho already explains.
rho_grid <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.02)
acme_rho <- vapply(rho_grid, function(r) {
  b_adj <- unname(coef(y_fit)["M"]) - r * s_y / s_m
  a_hat * b_adj
}, numeric(1))

k        <- which.min(abs(acme_rho))
rho_star <- rho_grid[k]
c(rho_star = rho_star, acme_at_rho_star = round(acme_rho[k], 4))
#>         rho_star acme_at_rho_star 
#>            0.800           -0.001
Code
plot(rho_grid, acme_rho, type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "#4477aa",
     xlab = "rho (mediator-outcome error correlation)",
     ylab = "estimated ACME")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
abline(v = rho_star, lty = 3, col = "#bb5566")
text(rho_star, max(acme_rho) * 0.9,
     labels = paste0("rho* = ", rho_star), pos = 4)

In this configuration the indirect effect survives until \(\rho\) is large, on the order of 0.8, so the conclusion is not fragile to modest mediator-outcome confounding. That is a claim a reader can check against the explanatory power of the observed covariates: if no measured covariate comes close to a residual correlation of 0.8, an unmeasured one probably does not either. “The results are robust” carries none of this information.

The mechanism-off contrast is a different kind of evidence. Suppose a regime \(W=1\) in which the treatment can no longer move the mediator, because accurate information replaces the biased signal, while everything else about the population is held fixed. The indirect effect should vanish there, and the contrast across regimes is the quantity the argument turns on.

Code
W  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)                    # 1 = accurate reading available
# The D -> M path operates only when the biased signal is the clinician's input.
M2 <- a_true * D * (1 - W) + gam_M * U + rnorm(n)
Y2 <- c_true * D + b_true * M2 + gam_Y * U + rnorm(n)

indirect_by_regime <- vapply(c(0, 1), function(w) {
  idx <- W == w
  a_w <- coef(lm(M2[idx] ~ D[idx]))[2]
  b_w <- coef(lm(Y2[idx] ~ D[idx] + M2[idx]))[3]
  unname(a_w * b_w)
}, numeric(1))

names(indirect_by_regime) <- c("mechanism on (W=0)", "mechanism off (W=1)")
round(indirect_by_regime, 3)
#>  mechanism on (W=0) mechanism off (W=1) 
#>               0.343              -0.034

The estimate under \(W=1\) is near zero while the estimate under \(W=0\) is not, and the gap between them is what a rival explanation must also reproduce. Both halves matter: the sensitivity sweep tells the reader how much unmeasured confounding the level result can absorb, and the mechanism-off contrast tells the reader whether the proposed channel, rather than some other channel correlated with it, is the one carrying the effect.

44.10 Selection on Unobservables: A Worked Oster Bound

Every design that relies on selection on observables faces the same referee question: the coefficient barely moved when you added controls, so what? Stability alone means little. If the controls explain almost none of the outcome, the coefficient would not move whether or not omitted variables matter. Oster (2019) turns the intuition into a number. It scales the coefficient’s movement by the movement in \(R^2\) and asks how much more the unobservables would have to matter than the observables to drive the estimate to zero.

Let \(\mathring\beta\) and \(\mathring R\) be the coefficient and \(R^2\) from the short regression, and \(\tilde\beta\) and \(\tilde R\) the same from the regression with controls. Let \(R_{\max}\) be the \(R^2\) a regression would reach if the unobservables could be included too, and let \(\delta\) be the selection on unobservables relative to observables. The approximate bias-adjusted coefficient is

\[ \beta^{*}\approx\tilde\beta-\delta\,(\mathring\beta-\tilde\beta)\, \frac{R_{\max}-\tilde R}{\tilde R-\mathring R}, \tag{44.30}\]

and setting \(\beta^{*}=0\) gives the \(\delta\) that would erase the effect. Oster suggests \(R_{\max}=1.3\,\tilde R\), a cutoff calibrated so that most randomized results in her sample of published studies survive it. Treat it as a convention, not a theorem.

A worked case comes from Griffin, Kruger, and Mahajan (2026), who regress ZIP-code fraud on social proximity to fraud elsewhere (Section 52.5.1). Both regressions include county fixed effects. Adding demographic controls moves the standardized coefficient from 1.054 to 0.982 and the \(R^2\) from 0.699 to 0.729. The paper reports the bound at \(R_{\max}=0.90\) and \(R_{\max}=1\). Table 44.12 reproduces both and adds Oster’s default. Its inputs come from our re-estimation of their Table 4 with the authors’ replication package (Griffin, Kruger, and Mahajan 2025).

Code
b_short <- 1.0540091; r_short <- 0.6989463   # county FE only
b_ctrl  <- 0.9823109; r_ctrl  <- 0.7294715    # + demographic controls

rmax <- c(0.90, 1.3 * r_ctrl, 1.00)
shift <- (b_short - b_ctrl) * (rmax - r_ctrl) / (r_ctrl - r_short)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    R_max = c("0.90 (paper)", sprintf("%.3f (Oster default)", 1.3 * r_ctrl), "1.00 (paper)"),
    beta_star = round(b_ctrl - shift, 3),
    delta_for_zero = round(b_ctrl / shift, 2)
  ),
  col.names = c("$R_{\\max}$", "$\\beta^*$ at $\\delta = 1$", "$\\delta$ that sets $\\beta^* = 0$")
)

The paper’s footnote reports 0.582 and 0.347, and the arithmetic reproduces both. Four lessons follow from the case.

  • The \(R^2\) moved only 0.03 while the coefficient moved 0.07. That ratio is why the bias-adjusted estimate falls so far, from 0.98 to as low as 0.35. Small coefficient movement is reassuring only when the controls also add explanatory power.
  • The choice of \(R_{\max}\) decides the answer. At Oster’s default (\(0.948\)), the bound is 0.468, below the paper’s preferred value and above its extreme one. Report the bound across a range of \(R_{\max}\), or report the \(\delta\) that zeroes the effect, so readers can apply their own threshold. Here that \(\delta\) runs from 1.55 to 2.45.
  • The short regression already includes county fixed effects. The bound therefore speaks only to selection within counties, beyond the fixed effects. That is the right comparison for this design, but say which baseline you used, because the bound changes with it.
  • Use plain \(R^2\), not adjusted \(R^2\), from regressions on the same sample with the same weights. Mixing samples, as happens when controls have missing values, makes the ratio meaningless.

Equation 44.30 is the approximation used in the paper. Oster’s Stata command psacalc solves the exact version, which can differ when \(\delta\) is far from 1. Both rest on proportional selection: the unobservables relate to the treatment the way the observables do, scaled by \(\delta\). A referee who thinks the omitted variable is unlike any included control, such as targeted advertising that follows social ties, can reject that premise.

44.11 Choosing a Design

No design dominates; each buys identification with a different assumption, and the right choice depends on what variation the world (or the firm) supplies. The comparison below summarizes the trade-offs.

Three principles guide the choice in marketing practice. First, prefer experimentation where the cost of running it is bearable; in advertising and pricing, firms increasingly hold out geographies or randomize at the user level precisely because the observational alternatives are so unreliable (Gordon et al. 2019b). Second, when an experiment is infeasible, match the design to the source of exogenous variation: a sharp eligibility rule invites RD, a staggered rollout invites DiD, a jurisdictional boundary cutting through common economic geography invites a boundary discontinuity (Section 44.7.2), a single large treated entity invites SCM, and a credible supply-side shifter invites IV. Third, triangulate: where two designs with different assumptions point to the same answer, the causal claim is far more credible than any single estimate, because the assumptions fail for different reasons. Figure 44.14 condenses these principles into the decision sequence an analyst walks.

44.12 Threats Common to All Designs

Beyond design-specific failures, several threats recur and deserve a standing checklist. Spillovers and general equilibrium: a treatment that changes one unit’s behavior may change untreated units’ behavior (SUTVA failure), and a price experiment that would be profitable at small scale may not survive a firm-wide rollout once competitors and supply respond. Attrition and survivorship: differential dropout between arms reintroduces selection even into a randomized design. Outcome windows and dynamics: advertising and brand effects accumulate and decay, so an effect measured over too short a window understates the true return; carryover (the Koyck/adstock structure of Chapter 14) must be modeled, not assumed away. Multiple comparisons: testing many metrics, segments, or variants inflates false positives, demanding pre-registration of primary outcomes or explicit correction. External validity: every estimand here is local to a population, a period, and a level of treatment intensity; a LATE for compliers, an RD effect at a cutoff, or an SCM effect for one market need not transfer to the firm’s broader decision. Naming the estimand—the discipline this chapter opened with—is the antidote, because it forces the analyst to state precisely whose effect, under what intervention, has been estimated.

44.13 Foundational vs. frontier at a glance

The seminar marks every method as foundational (qualifying-exam material the left column) or frontier (where dissertations are written, the right column). The marketing-specific value-add over a generic econometrics course is concentrated in Weeks 12–14—advertising measurement, incrementality/geo/pricing experiments, and marketplace interference—and in framing every method around small effects, non-stationary platforms, and targeting decisions.

Block Foundational core [F] Frontier extensions [R]
Framework (Wk 1) Rubin 1974; Holland 1986; Imbens–Rubin design- vs. model-based inference
Experiments / A/B (Wk 2) Fisher/Neyman inference; Kohavi time-series/switchback; always-valid inference
Selection on observables (Wk 3) CIA, bad controls, overlap (Angrist–Pischke) sensitivity analysis; Athey–Imbens overview
IV (Wk 4) Imbens–Angrist LATE; Angrist–Imbens–Rubin weak-IV; judge/shift-share designs
DiD I (Wk 5) Card–Krueger; Bertrand–Duflo–Mullainathan wild-cluster inference
DiD II — staggered (Wk 6) the critique itself is now foundational Goodman-Bacon; CS; dCDH; Sun–Abraham; BJS; Roth et al.
RDD (Wk 7) Imbens–Lemieux guide Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik robust inference
Synthetic control (Wk 8) Abadie–Diamond–Hainmueller; Abadie JEL synthetic DiD; gsynth; CausalImpact
Panel/event-study (Wk 9) FE/FD (Wooldridge) design-based panel experiments; matrix completion
Matching/weighting (Wk 10) Rosenbaum–Rubin; Hirano–Imbens–Ridder approximate residual balancing; PS-matching inference
ML for HTE (Wk 11) Athey–Imbens causal trees causal forests; GRF; double/debiased ML
Ad measurement (Wk 12) Lewis–Rao unfavorable economics ghost ads; experiments-vs-observational (Gordon et al.)
Incrementality/geo/pricing (Wk 13) Blake–Nosko–Tadelis; Anderson–Simester targeting-policy evaluation; bandit pricing
Interference (Wk 14) Manski reflection problem Aronow–Samii; Sävje et al.; graph-cluster designs

Week 6 is the rare case where a critique has itself become foundational: no student can use DiD today without knowing the staggered-adoption failure of the two-way fixed-effects estimator. A paper is promoted from frontier to foundational only once it is standard qualifying-exam material—the staggered-DiD critique is the current example mid-transition.

44.14 How this chapter expands

This chapter is a living syllabus. Future revisions should (1) reconcile this canonical ordering against actual week-by-week reading lists pulled from live PhD syllabi (MIT applied econometrics, Chicago Booth’s causal-inference and quantitative-marketing sequences, Stanford GSB/Econ causal-ML courses, Berkeley digital-experiments, and the Wharton/Columbia/Kellogg marketing-methods seminars), citing program and URL; (2) track Week 6, which moves fastest, as the robust-DiD literature consolidates (continuous treatment, non-absorbing treatment, triple-difference, design-based DiD); (3) deepen the marketing-platform core of Weeks 12–14 with incrementality and geo-experiment methodology as version-of-record DOIs appear (much of it currently lives in working papers and platform tech reports), plus the growing experimentation-under-interference literature for marketplaces and recommender systems; (4) add a power/design appendix on MDE/power for small-lift ad experiments, variance reduction (CUPED), cluster-randomization power loss, and sequential testing; (5) add a software/replication appendix mapping methods to canonical packages (grf, DoubleML/econml, did, fixest/sunab, rdrobust, Synth/synthdid/gsynth, CausalImpact); and (6) maintain the foundational/frontier marking as the load-bearing pedagogical device.

44.15 Key Takeaways

  • A causal effect is a comparison of potential outcomes (Equation 44.1); because only one is observed per unit (Equation 44.2), every estimate rests on an assumption that recovers the missing counterfactual.
  • The naive treated-minus-untreated difference is biased by selection (Equation 44.3); randomization removes the bias by construction, which is why field experiments and A/B tests are the benchmark.
  • In advertising, the effect is small relative to sales volatility, so experiments must be very large to be conclusive and observational substitutes can err by multiples or in sign (Lewis and Rao 2015; Gordon et al. 2019b).
  • Each quasi-experimental design targets a specific estimand under a specific assumption—DiD/ATT under parallel trends, IV/LATE under exclusion, RD under continuity, SCM/ATT under donor pre-fit—and each has a named diagnostic and a named failure mode (Table 44.13).
  • Boundary discontinuities replace the running variable with a location: units on either side of an administrative line share economic geography but not the treatment (Section 44.7.2). Manipulation is rarely the threat; coincident boundaries are, because administrative lines arrive bundled with tax, licensing, and regulatory changes, and adjacency invites spillovers across the line (Canayaz and Gustafson 2026).
  • Name the estimand before choosing a method, probe the identifying assumption with its diagnostic, and triangulate across designs whose assumptions fail for different reasons.
  • Mechanism is a separate identification problem. The indirect effect (Equation 44.26) is defined by a cross-world counterfactual, so it requires sequential ignorability (Equation 44.28–Equation 44.29), and randomizing the treatment supplies only the first half (Imai, Keele, and Yamamoto 2010; Bullock, Green, and Ha 2010). A clean total effect does not buy a clean mechanism.
  • A pathway argument is defended by manipulating the mediator, finding a condition that switches the mechanism off, signing the direction of the residual bias, and reporting the confounding strength at which the conclusion flips—not by adding a third regression. Zhang and Jetley (2026) is a compact example: pulse-oximetry measurement bias is traced from race to undertreatment to unplanned ICU readmission, with the availability of an accurate arterial reading serving as the moderator under which the disparity is predicted—and found—to vanish (Section 44.9.4).
  • In a moderated mediation, the path the moderator sits on is the hypothesis: Model 7 (moderating \(D \to M\)) and Model 14 (moderating \(M \to Y\)) assert different theories and are not interchangeable (Hayes 2017). Test the claim with the index of moderated mediation, not with a table of conditional effects at ±1 SD, because a difference in significance is not a significant difference; read constituent terms in the interaction model as conditional effects at moderator zero; and treat any crossover threshold as an estimate with sampling error rather than a managerial cutoff (Section 44.9.6).

44.16 Further Reading

The potential-outcomes framework and the estimators in this chapter are developed at length in the standard graduate econometrics references (Cameron and Trivedi 2005; Greene 2003) and in the econometric treatments of program evaluation (Heckman and Vytlacil 2007; Abbring and Heckman 2007). For demand estimation with endogenous prices and instruments built from rival product characteristics, the differentiated-products literature is the entry point (Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes 1995). The advertising-measurement evidence that motivates experimentation over observational inference is most directly accessible through the large-scale experimental comparisons cited above (Lewis, Rao, and Reiley 2011; Lewis and Rao 2015; Gordon et al. 2019b), and the dynamics of advertising response that complicate any single-window estimate are treated in Chapter 14. On boundary discontinuities, Canayaz and Gustafson (2026) is a compact worked example—contiguous-county comparisons across federal judicial circuits, with the exit-versus-relocation decomposition that shows what the design can separate; its substantive reading is in Section 30.6.

On mechanism, the classical procedure and its vocabulary come from Baron and Kenny (1986), and the potential-outcomes reconstruction that gives the indirect effect a causal definition, an identifying assumption, and a sensitivity analysis is developed in Imai, Keele, and Yamamoto (2010) and Imai, Keele, and Tingley (2010); Imai, Tingley, and Yamamoto (2013) sets out the experimental designs—parallel, crossover, encouragement—that identify a mechanism rather than assume one. Bullock, Green, and Ha (2010) is the sharpest short statement of why a randomized treatment does not buy a randomized mediator. For the moderated-mediation estimand and the conditional indirect effect, see Preacher, Rucker, and Hayes (2007). Zhang and Jetley (2026) is the worked design read in Section 44.9.4, and the underlying clinical measurement bias is documented in Sjoding et al. (2020).

The primary sources behind each design are worth reading in the order the chapter develops them. The potential-outcomes framework itself is Rubin (1974), which is where the notation of this chapter originates and where the stability assumption that everything else leans on is first made explicit. For instrumental variables, Imbens and Angrist (1994) and Angrist, Imbens, and Rubin (1996) establish that an instrument identifies a local average treatment effect defined on compliers rather than the population average — the single most misread result in applied work — and the weak-instrument diagnostics that decide whether that identification is worth anything come from Staiger and Stock (1997).

Difference-in-differences has two separate literatures a reader must not conflate. The inference problem — serially correlated outcomes making conventional standard errors far too small — is Bertrand, Duflo, and Mullainathan (2004), and the design’s canonical application is Card and Krueger (1994). The identification problem under staggered adoption is newer and more damaging: with treatment timing varying across units and effects varying over time, the two-way fixed-effects estimator averages some comparisons with negative weights and can return an estimate of the wrong sign (Goodman-Bacon 2021), which is why the group-time estimators of Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) should now be the default rather than the robustness check.

For regression discontinuity, Imbens and Lemieux (2008) and David S. Lee and Lemieux (2010) are the practical guides — bandwidth choice, polynomial order, covariate balance — and McCrary (2008) supplies the density test that decides whether units sorted across the threshold, which is the assumption the whole design rests on. When no discontinuity and no natural comparison group exist, the synthetic-control construction of Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2010) builds a weighted comparison unit from a donor pool, with the pre-treatment fit serving as its own diagnostic.

On the experimental side, the marketing field’s cleanest demonstrations that observational advertising estimates diverge sharply from experimental ones are Gordon et al. (2019a) and its follow-on Gordon et al. (2021), while Shapiro, Hitsch, and Tuchman (2021) shows how little survives when the same design is replicated across hundreds of brands rather than one. For pricing specifically, Anderson and Simester (2003) remains the model of a field experiment that isolates a single design parameter. Finally, anyone running continuously monitored online experiments should understand why repeatedly checking a fixed-horizon test inflates the false-positive rate well beyond its nominal level, and adopt a sequential or always-valid procedure instead — the peeking problem is not a rare edge case but the default behavior of most experimentation dashboards.
